articles.title: 'Layer upon layer of miracles': How Nepal flood survivors were rescued from tunnel
articles.summary: From searching for a buried tunnel entrance to blowing up rocks the size of cars, rescuers had to surmount multiple challenges to reach survivors.

blocks.text: A tunnelling expert involved in the rescue operation at a blocked Nepalese hydropower tunnel has described to the BBC how they managed to reach survivors.

Arnold Dix has been advising Nepal's hydropower authorities on how to dig through the blocked tunnel to Trishuli 3A Hydropower Station, which was one of several stations hit by last week's massive flash flood on the Nepal-Tibet border.
"It's like layer upon layer of layer of miracles" that they found two men on Friday, he said, given that the multiple challenges they faced.
The first hurdle was to locate the hydropower station, in a landscape rendered nearly unrecognisable by the flood that has so far killed 1,300 people.

"I've never known an rescue operation where you had to look for an entrance of a tunnel that was previously up the hill, that was now underground. You can imagine the enormity of the avalanche, it completely buried the entrance," said Dix, who is the president of the International Tunnelling and Underground Space Association.

Using engineering techniques, old topographic maps, satellite imagery of the area after the disaster, video footage from helicopters, and "anything else we could find on the surface of the mountain such as power poles", Dix and his team triangulated the likely position of the entrance and started digging.
They found it - but the next challenge was to locate the survivors.
"We knew they would be up ahead, but we didn't know where exactly. So you just have to start digging in the right direction. And you listen out if you can hear anybody," he said.
Rescuers had to get through a tunnel blocked entirely by mud and rocks - some bigger than cars - and had to resort to using explosives to clear the way.
"We had to use explosives which we normally never do because of the risk of blowing up people [trapped in the tunnel] and blowing ourselves up," said Dix.
He credited the Nepalese army for doing "a wonderful job" in managing the explosions with precision to ensure they would not destabilise the tunnel.
At the same time, they discovered the tunnel was still full of water.
Using excavators and pumping machines, Nepalese rescuers dug a series of trenches from the tunnel all the way to the river outside, so they could drain the water.
Finally, they had to dig a passageway, "a tiny tunnel the size of a person", through the debris at the top of the tunnel.
The advantage of this location "is that you can use the original tunnel's roof as your little tunnel's roof. Also, it mitigates risk of flooding," said Dix.
In the early hours of Friday morning, rescuers heard what they thought could be voices.
According to local reports, they called out "don't worry, we're here to rescue you" - and heard back a faint "okay".
Shortly after that, they pulled out Sanjaya Shah and Kabir Maharjan, alive.
But with dozens of people still thought to be trapped inside the tunnel, the work is far from over.
Dix estimated that they had dug about 60m from the entrance by now, and they would need to dig another 150m more to reach the hydropower station located deep inside the mountain.

Rescuers are hoping that the debris from the flood would not have reached the station, because if it did, "there would be all kinds of complications - anybody in the station could have been hit by rocks and mud or it could be flooded".
The team on the ground are still facing significant dangers.

"Up ahead, even now, we might run into water which would drown the people tunnelling," said Dix. "And we also have the risk of another flood outside happening, so water could come from behind. So there's the risk of facing water on both ends."
But, buoyed by Friday's successful rescue, the team is now hopeful it will reach more survivors in time.
"It's a big relief, that we are on the right track. And it gives us renewed energy that our thinking [on how to conduct the rescue] works... we have never done something like this before."
Dix said they are now heading towards what he called the "Goldilocks zone" which would be "more friendly to life".
This zone is at the uppermost level of the hydropower station where there is some space where survivors may be located.
"We got two people out. If we were playing at a casino, some might say it's time to walk away, but we say game on, time to take on the house."

blocks.text: Live
The newly launched satellite will hover some 36,000 kilometers above Earth and is being called India's "eye in the sky." DW has the latest.

blocks.caption: It is the first time India has launched an imaging satellite into geosynchronous (GEO) orbitImage: ANI/IMAGO

blocks.text: What you need to know

items: India has carried out a successful launch of its EOS-05 Earth observation satellite

Air India begins voluntary testing for all its pilots after probe agency finds drug test of a captain "non-negative" in August air incident

blocks.text: Here is a roundup of the latest developments from India on Friday, September 4.
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
September 4, 2026
India launches key Earth observation satellite
The Indian Space Research Organization (ISRO) on Friday successfully deployed the country's first ever imaging satellite in geosynchronous orbit.

A Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV) — carrying the EOS-05 Earth observation satellite — lifted off from ISRO's primary spaceport, the Satish Dhawan Space Center in Sriharikota, at 2:55 a.m. local time (2125 UTC).
The Indian space agency shared visuals of the countdown for the launch which ended with the GSLV-F17 firing up and lifting off, lighting up the dark early morning skies in its wake.
About 18 minutes later, ISRO announced that the satellite was successfully placed in the intended sub-geosynchronous transfer orbit.
ISRO proclaimed "Mission Success!" in a post on X.
ISRO's first success in 2026

The launch marked the 19th flight of India's GSLV. It was also ISRO's first success this year after a mission setback in January saw a Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle rocket failing to place 16 satellites in the intended orbit
The EOS-05 — with a payload of over 2,300 kilograms — is the country's heaviest ever satellite to be carried by a GSLV.
The satellite — dubbed as India's "eye in the sky" — will operate from an altitude of roughly 36,000 kilometers above Earth, which is higher than typical low-Earth-orbit observation satellites
The satellite will match the home planet's rotational speed.
Its expected mandate is to bolster India's ability to obtain frequent imagery of large areas for applications including Earth observation and monitoring.
"The health of the satellite is perfectly alright," ISRO Chairman V Narayanan said after the launch.
PM Modi lauds India's growing space capabilities
On Friday, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi hailed the satellite's launch as "yet another outstanding achievement" by the Indian space agency and "a proud moment" for the country.

"The successful launch of GSLV-F17 carrying EOS-05, India's first-ever imaging satellite from Geosynchronous orbit is a reflection of the excellence, innovation and growing capabilities that define India's space sector," he said on X.

articles.title: 2026 Beethoven Festival evokes a sense of home
articles.summary: The motto of this year's festival in Bonn is "Home/At Home," featuring musicians from diverse cultures presenting pieces from their homelands.

image.caption: After 10 years, the Beethovenfest in Bonn returns to its old home, the BeethovenhalleImage: Marc John/Bonn.digital/picture alliance

blocks.text: Four trumpeters will be scattered throughout the concert hall, accompanied by organ music, promising a magnificent auditory experience in Bonn's newly renovated Beethovenhalle.

The piece "A Call to the Heavens" was composed by Stefan Behrisch specifically for the opening of this year's Beethovenfest. Additionally, the London Symphony Orchestra, led by principal conductor Sir Antonio Pappano, will perform Ludwig van Beethoven's "Die Weihe des Hauses" ("The Consecration of the House") as well as Bruckner's Symphony No. 9 at the opening concert on September 4.

blocks.caption: The Beethovenhalle aims to make everyone feel at home Image: Marc John/Bonn.digital/picture alliance

blocks.text: For nine years, Bonn's Beethovenhalle, a designated historic landmark, was unavailable for the festival. But now, as Philipp Seliger, spokesperson for the Beethoven Festival explains, "we have a large concert hall again with its excellent original acoustics." He adds: "We can once again invite major renowned orchestras because we have the appropriate stage and infrastructure." This also prompted Hungarian star pianist, András Schiff, to perform at the festival this year.
A musical home for everyone

blocks.caption: Juri de Marco founded a community choir in Bonn's Tannenbusch neighborhoodImage: Beethovenfest Bonn

blocks.text: The new hall is not only intended to make stars and major orchestras feel at home — the audience and local musicians ought to feel that way too. Indeed, for local musicians, there is a specially designed "Festival Salon" where local communities and bands can create their own programs. And anyone can come by and participate in the "Meet your band" project, which is an accessible, free program for people who otherwise wouldn't visit a classical concert hall.

The Beethovenfest also reaches out to people in neighborhoods across the city, right where they live. For over a year, as a part of this effort, Juri de Marco and the "Community Choir" have been encouraging people to sing and improvise, regardless of whether they can read music.

blocks.caption: Steven Walter addresses the topic of home not only in his music, but also in lectures and in discussion forumsImage: Bjorn Kietzmann/DW

blocks.text: "For me, home is more a feeling than it is a place. It's where you can rely on a genuine social network, where people notice when you are absent," says festival director Steven Walter. who has lived in various places around the world himself. "Everywhere I go, my sense of well-being depends on my social connections."
Beethoven reinterpreted

Ludwig van Beethoven was born in Bonn in 1850, and died in Vienna in 1827. Next year marks the 200th anniversary of his death, and to celebrate it, pianist Kit Armstrong with conductor Jan Caeyers, along with his orchestra "Le Concert Olympique," are launching "Beethoven 27," a major Beethoven cycle. In nine concerts, they will present entirely new interpretations of Beethoven's nine symphonies, as well as his sonatas and piano concertos.

blocks.caption: 'Beethoven 27' is the name of the project in which Kit Armstrong plays the pianoImage: SALVATORE DI NOLFI/KEYSTONE/picture alliance

blocks.text: The first three concerts will be presented at this year's Beethovenfest. Caeyers has devoted himself to Beethoven not only as a conductor but also as a musicologist. He is the author of the acclaimed biography "Beethoven: A life." Even so, Caeyers says he is far from finished discovering the composer.

"Every time I immerse myself in Beethoven, new and unexpected doors open. That's what keeps me fascinated," Caeyers told DW. Pianist Kit Armstrong feels the same way. "There isn't just one Beethoven," he said. "There are countless images and perspectives of Beethoven, including many that emerged long after his death. Those perspectives should also inform the way we interpret his music today."
Spotlight on Georgia

This year's Beethovenfest artists will introduce music from their homelands. Among them are Senegalese kora player Momi Maiga and Palestinian-Syrian pianist Aeham Ahmad, who gained global renown for playing the piano amid the rubble of the Syrian civil war.

blocks.caption: Violinist Lisa Batiashvili also supports young talent from her native Georgia, including composer Tsotne Zedginidze Image: picture-alliance/dpa/P. Zinken

blocks.text: Violinist Lisa Batiashvili, who was born in Georgia, is this year's artist in residence at the Beethovenfest. Performing with the Dresden Philharmonic, she will present works from her homeland as part of the program "City Lights" — a personal tribute to Georgia, which the festival is spotlighting this year.

As part of the festival's long-running "Campus" youth exchange program, young musicians from Georgia and Germany will collaborate, with Beethoven's music being performed alongside works by leading Georgian composers. The entire ensemble will also perform Heinrich Schütz's five-part motet "Verleih uns Frieden gnädiglich" ("Grant Us Gracious Peace").

Musicians from Germany's National Youth Orchestra and the Tbilisi Youth Orchestra held their joint rehearsal residency in June, developing their own artistic vision and program for Beethovenfest. The project also explores how young artists see themselves in a country facing political turmoil, where the path toward Europe has repeatedly shifted course.

blocks.caption: During rehearsals in Tbilisi, conductor Mirian Khukhunaishvili (left) and composer Tsotne Zedginidze (right) discuss his new workImage: Beethovenfest

blocks.text: 17-year-old composer and pianist Tsotne Zedginidze is regarded as one of Georgia's most extraordinary young musical talents. He was commissioned to write the Campus project's new work.
Beyond classical music

Crossovers, musical fusion and new ideas for the future of music remain central to this year's Beethovenfest. Two musical worlds will come together with kora player Momi Maiga joining the string orchestra "Ensemble Resonanz" to improvise on Beethoven's music.

blocks.caption: Composer and performer Brittany J. Green combines sound, video, movement and text in her workImage: Adley Haywood

blocks.text: American composer Brittany J. Green will experiment with artificial intelligence and visual effects in her work "gLitchED dreams//invisible BEINGS." Performed with the music collective "Alarm Will Sound," the piece creates a sonic landscape inspired by the digital age. "We're looking for the Beethovens of our time," says Philipp Seliger, "including people who aren't necessarily composers of classical music."
The Beethovenfest runs from Sept 3 through Oct 3, 2026. DW is a media partner and co-shareholder of the festival.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Remulla: Sara Duterte’s camp to post bail in grave threats case
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The camp of Vice President Sara Duterte intends to post bail in the grave threats case against her on Friday, according to Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla. In a text message,…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The camp of Vice President Sara Duterte intends to post bail in the grave threats case against her on Friday, according to Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla.
In a text message, Remulla told the Inquirer that Duterte’s lawyers “confirmed that they received the warrant.”
“They intend to post bail ASAP (as soon as possible),” he noted.
In a statement earlier on Friday, Duterte’s legal counsel Paul Lawrence Lim said the Quezon City Regional Trial Court had issued a warrant to arrest Duterte for grave threats.
Duterte’s camp has yet to answer reporters’ queries on whether they would post bail.
The warrant sets bail at P120,000 each for three counts of grave threats in relation to Section 6 of Republic Act No. 10175 or the Cybercrime Prevention Act, for a total of P360,000.
Duterte was charged with grave threats by the National Bureau of Investigation last August.

The case stemmed from her statements against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr, First Lady Liza Araneta Marcos, and former House Speaker Martin Romualdez during a virtual press conference in November 2024./coa

articles.title: Ridon: Sara Duterte arrest case separate from impeachment
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — House of Representatives prosecutor and Bicol Saro party-list Rep. Terry Ridon said that the criminal case against Vice President Sara Duterte is separate from her impeachment…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — House of Representatives prosecutor and Bicol Saro party-list Rep. Terry Ridon said that the criminal case against Vice President Sara Duterte is separate from her impeachment proceedings, noting that the prosecution panel will continue to press on.

Ridon on Friday said that the arrest warrant against Duterte is “not, by itself, a determination of guilt” and that the vice president “will have every opportunity to present her defenses before the proper court.”
“The impeachment proceedings are a separate constitutional accountability process. The Senate Impeachment Court will independently determine the matters properly before it,” he said.

Ridon made the statement as Duterte’s lawyer announced that a warrant of arrest was issued by the Quezon City Regional Trial Court this Friday over Duterte’s grave threats case before the National Bureau of Investigation.

He said the prosecution team took note of Duterte’s counsel’s statement, saying that the vice president has no intention of evading the law and will avail herself of the legal remedies available to her.

Duterte’s warrant came as her impeachment trial before the Senate is ongoing. In her impeachment trial, the vice president is likewise accused of culpable violation of the Constitution and betrayal of public trust for allegedly making kill threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta Marcos, and former House Speaker Martin Romualdez, among others./coa

articles.title: VP Sara camp receives arrest warrant over grave threats, plans bail ASAP - DILG
articles.summary: The lawyers of Vice President Sara Duterte have received the arrest warrant against her and are planning to post bail as soon as possible, Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla said on Friday. “Their…

blocks.text: Published September 4, 2026 4:00pm
The lawyers of Vice President Sara Duterte have received the arrest warrant against her and are planning to post bail as soon as possible, Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla said on Friday.
“Their lawyers confirmed that they received the warrant and they intend to post bail ASAP,” Remulla told reporters in a message.
The Quezon City (QC) Regional Trial Court has issued an arrest warrant against Duterte over three counts of grave threats.
Bail has been set at P120,000 for each count.

In a statement, the Department of Justice said it "notes the Resolution issued today, 04 September 2026, by Branch 98 of the RTC of Quezon City denying the motion by the accused Vice President Sara Z. Duterte to defer or recall the warrant of arrest against her in the criminal case for grave threats."
"In the same Resolution, the Court found probable cause to hold the accused for trial on all three counts of Grave Threats and ordered the issuance of a warrant of arrest," the DOJ said.
"The Department respects the Court’s ruling and reaffirms its commitment to the rule of law," it added,
Duterte's lawyer said she had no intention of evading the law.

"Regardless of the question on jurisdiction, she has no intention of evading the law and will continue to exercise all her legal remedies," Duterte’s counsel, Atty. Paul Lawrence Lim said in a statement.

In early August, the DOJ filed three counts of grave threats against Duterte over her remarks that she hired an individual to kill President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta Marcos, and former speaker Martin Romualdez, should an alleged plot against her succeed.
The Vice President filed a motion to quash on the ground of jurisdiction, arguing that she and other impeachable officers have limited procedural immunity while in office under the 1987 Constitution.
The court held oral arguments on the motion in August.
Duterte previously said that her remarks were "maliciously taken out of logical context."
She also clarified that her "assassination" statement was not a threat, saying she only highlighted the alleged threat to her security. –NB, GMA News

articles.title: Ryan Reynolds, Kenneth Branagh-starring Mayday takes on Russia. And America
articles.summary: It would be depressing for a movie like Mayday to work, given that it's really just a form of propaganda. Which makes it all the more difficult to admit that Mayday, starring Kenneth Branagh and Ryan…

image.caption: Kenneth Branagh, left, and Ryan Reynolds star in Apple TV's Mayday, a movie that boldly asks: What if Russians were people, too? (Apple TV)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

It would be depressing for a movie like Mayday to work, given that it's really just a form of propaganda. Which makes it all the more difficult to admit that Mayday, starring Kenneth Branagh and Ryan Reynolds, actually does completely work.
Apple TV film about a U.S. navy pilot behind enemy lines in Russia is worth a watch
It's odd that we keep having to learn that other humans are people, too.

In fact, you could call it an indictment of humanity, or just of our age, that the premise of Mayday — a 1980s American serviceman slowly coming to terms with the idea that a Soviet soldier actually has a subjective inner life and thoughts other than consuming babies — works at all.

It's presented as hard to accept that aging ex-KGB agent Nikolai (Kenneth Branagh) has non-dastardly intentions for rescuing U.S. navy pilot Troy (Ryan Reynolds) when he crashes near Nikolai’s cabin deep in U.S.S.R. territory. And when he escorts Troy through hails of Cold War gunfire and haymaker punches out of empathy and altruism, these qualities are framed, at least initially, as strange and alien — coming, as they do, from a Russian in 1987.

It's also based on the assumption that a reasonable person wouldn't believe Nikolai's soft-hearted, America-loving reason for protecting the wounded Troy, who represents the country he's come to love. Especially because he has his own estranged daughter (Maria Bakalova) to find and protect — not to mention they now have a rogue KGB agent (Marcin Dorociński) and his shadowy cabal of ruthless killers on their trail.

Are you really going to trust that it’s all because Nikolai just plain loves America and wants to defect, rather than it being an elaborate ruse to infiltrate and take down that shining city upon a hill from the inside.

It's somewhat embarrassing, though not unexpected, that the rest of the film does play out as if to show salt-of-the-earth American Troy that foreigners can be just as genuine, complex and conscious as he is.

Mayday and other movies like it only work if we admit it makes implicit sense to not only hate anyone that's different from you, but to assume that — at least at first — those people are barely people at all.
Which makes it all the more difficult to admit that Mayday actually does completely work.

It's a shoot-em-up, odd-couple buddy comedy with more style than it has any excuse for, and features both actors in top form: Branagh as the charismatically kind death machine, and Reynolds as the straight-man foil who's desperately trying to keep up and, generally, away from the carnage.

And importantly, there’s just enough of that carnage to match its comedy — and little enough of the latter to keep it from getting stale. Because positioning Reynolds as the wisecracking sidekick is always preferable to movies that situate his Deadpool-esque, wink-wink, nudge-nudge antics as the central selling point.

When those smarmy, self-satisfied asides come from the dead-inside side character in Adventureland, they play as both cute and revealing. But when The Adam Project decides to set a whole movie around snide sarcasm you quickly crash into the concept of diminishing returns.
Of course, it’s not the first time a director got the Reynolds balance right.

In truth, Mayday feels like a perfect mix between his 2015 tragicomic roadtrip comedy Mississippi Grind with sad-eyed Ben Mendelsohn, and his straight-shooting 2012 thriller Safe House alongside Denzel Washington as a similarly terrifying espionage everyman.

Mayday directors Jonathan Goldstein and John Francis Daley tack to the same narrative wind; not only does Branagh fill an equally sage, temporizing role, but the camera does, too. For every knock-down, drag-out, bloody-knuckles bar brawl we witness, we’re also treated to mostly long, sustained cuts.

The camera glides through the mayhem as unbothered and assured as Nikolai himself, pirouetting almost lazily around a relaxed Branagh as he relieves a man of the burden of having a face without shattered pieces of vodka bottle inside it.

It’s an impressive showcase of “less is more” camerawork — almost the exact opposite of the frenetic back and forth now seen in even modern Oscar winning movies. Instead, this camerawork is similar to the “slow is smooth, smooth is fast” martial art technique that Nikolai himself uses to put people in the hospital.

But the end result is still mostly simple and surface; an Olympus Has Fallen type of movie for the Reagan years. And, as mentioned, the heartening theme at its core only works if the idea of “people in Russia are people, too” wasn’t so laughably self-evident that it feels offensive.

But it’s far from the first piece of pop culture to mine that moral. Not too long ago, Netflix's Stranger Things doubled up on the trope, reflecting '80s trends seen in everything from heartrending Moscow on the Hudson to brain-numbing Russkies.
When they work, it’s because they aim for a vicarious, dramatic-irony thrill — how silly it that people once thought that way — or when they’re aware of their status as propaganda.

And propaganda they are; you’d be hard pressed to find a mainstream Western film that shows both America and Russia without depicting one as inherently good with some flaws and the other as a festering hellhole with a few moral (though emotionally vacant) resistors as the exception.

items: The only time The Dog Stars isn't boring is when it's bad
Insidious: Out of the Further swaps sadness for terror. Then forgets to terrorize

blocks.text: This is not to say propaganda is bad filmmaking — far from it. Above and beyond its military, American cultural exports are their most effective weapon; one that has conquered more nations than anything else in their arsenal.

But they can also showcase a rageful, entitled jingoism — the type of singular chosen-one narrative that birthed the weirdly terrifying, righteous violence of Red Dawn. Or that position it as such a bastion of humanity and freedom, that even the Russians end up cheering for America in Rocky IV.
But if there’s one thing to be said for Mayday, it's that it's at least dimly aware of its role in that system — and America’s.

Throughout, there's a back-and-forth between Nikolai and Troy on the respective propaganda they’ve been served. There are corrupt, ineffectual politicians on both sides abandoning their people. There are, of course, more egregious violations of rights perpetrated by the Soviets — but there isn’t a wholesale vilification of one, or wholesale vindication of the other.

In all, it’s a pretty low bar to clear. But it’s one that Mayday does lumber over, resulting in a mainstream American popcorn film that at least teases the question of whether there were clear cut good and bad guys in the Cold War.
It’s not much, but it’s enough to make one thing clear: The surprise isn’t discovering the humanity in the enemy, it's that we think we’re removed from it at all.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jackson Weaver is a reporter and film critic for CBC's entertainment news team in Toronto. You can reach him at jackson.weaver@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Health-care hiring has propped up Canada’s job market. Will patients see a difference?
articles.summary: A hiring boom across Alberta and Ontario health-care systems has been singlehandedly propping up Canada's national job market — but that growth may say more about the sluggish state of the rest of…

image.caption: Desjardins' analysis of provincial budget documents shows Alberta and Ontario each planned to spend upwards of $8 billion more on health in 2026 than 2025. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

blocks.text: A hiring boom across Alberta and Ontario health-care systems has been singlehandedly propping up Canada's national job market — but that growth may say more about the sluggish state of the rest of the economy than about improving patient outcomes.

A report from Desjardins Group looking at Statistics Canada jobs data shows the two provinces have collectively added over 100,000 health-care jobs, mainly in public institutions, since the early days of the U.S. trade war, a trend consistent with increased funding for the sector set aside in those provinces' budgets.

Desjardins' analysis of provincial budget documents shows Alberta and Ontario each planned to spend upwards of $8 billion more on health in 2026 than 2025. Ontario budgeted $91.5 billion for health last year while Alberta budgeted $24 billion.

Without that hiring, Canada's employment picture "would have been broadly flat," the report's author, Desjardins deputy chief economist Randall Bartlett, told CBC News — which he said means claims of a robust Canadian economy are "a little misguided."

Labour Force Survey data shows that since March 2025, there were nearly 133,000 jobs added nationwide in the health-care and social assistance sector — with hiring "most pronounced in hospitals and services for the elderly," the report notes — more than the 118,000 jobs added in all other sectors combined.

That concentrated hiring shows Alberta and Ontario following through on policies to increase spending "in the hope of expanding and supporting public health care," Bartlett said, with the end goal ideally playing out as tangible improvements to the system.

Whether that happens is another matter, however, with economists and health policy experts noting that more spending and job growth in health care don't automatically lead to better services for patients.

"It's really important to remember that just because a job is in the health-care sector, it does not mean that it's a job that's touching patients," said Fiona Clement, director of the Centre for Health Policy at the University of Calgary's Cummings School of Medicine.

items: Canada adds 75K jobs as economy rebounds from weak start to the year
Ontario seeks to connect 600,000 more people to primary care

blocks.text: In Alberta, where the government restructured its previous health authority into four separate agencies, "the entire support infrastructure of a ministry has to be replicated three more times," Clement said.
"Thinking about it at that level, it makes a lot of sense to me that there has been growth in that workforce."

There's less evidence that the new jobs have been in front-line patient care, Clement said, noting that College of Physicians and Surgeons of Alberta data shows "there has not been meaningful growth in the number of physicians in the province."
Alberta premier insists dual practice health care won't threaten public system

Some of the increased labour spending in Alberta and Ontario could merely be making up for slower hiring in the past, Bartlett noted — and some of the money will be going to wage increases for existing workers.
The provinces may also be preparing for demographic shifts on the horizon, said Livio Di Matteo, a professor of economics at Lakehead University who specializes in health economics and public policy.

"Large numbers of physicians are expected to retire over the next five years, as well as nurses and other types of health professionals," he said. "That's probably already starting up, which explains why there might be additional hiring or higher amounts of hiring."
Spending 'tends to go up'
Spending growth on its own, furthermore, is unremarkable, the experts said.

Government spending on health care generally increases over time because demand increases as populations grow, said Sara Allin, an associate professor of health policy at the University of Toronto and the director of the North American Observatory on Health Systems and Policies.
"We rarely see a real decline in spending. It tends to go up, often at a higher rate than economic growth," she said.
"Given that, we're going to expect more people to be hired."

How that plays out in province-wide networks can be quite complex, Allin noted, with regional populations evolving, services sometimes varying along rural-urban divides and some hospitals expanding while others face cuts.

"All these things can be true," she said. "It depends on where people are being hired, which hospitals facing deficits may be laying off, while others experiencing growth are hiring. It depends on the region and the capacity of the hospital to weather these financial pressures."
The population growth factor also means the health-care spending boom may not be as significant as it seems, said Di Matteo.

Data from the Canadian Institute for Health Information in 2025 shows that, with population growth and inflation factored in, spending growth per person in Alberta was around 0.3 per cent. In Ontario, it hovered around zero — "basically flat," he said.

Extrapolating recent population trends — the latest Statistics Canada data shows Ontario's population has declined for three straight quarters, while Alberta's has edged up — suggests Ontario's spending growth on a real per capita basis "should be growing," Bartlett said, and Alberta's would likely be "muted."
Rising per capita spending growth isn't a sure sign of an improving system, Clement said — and a drop in spending isn't necessarily bad.
"If you can spend less money per capita and get better outcomes, that means you're designing a system that is getting better value than before."
'No reason to think this will reverse'
Desjardins sees the hiring trend remaining strong "for the foreseeable future."

Both Alberta and Ontario have budgeted additional health-care spending "over the next couple of years," Desjardins' report says. With various factors likely to increase costs, and an aging population key among them, "there is no reason to think this will reverse."

items: Millions of Canadians struggle to get specialist health care: StatsCan report
Canada's oldest age group is also its fastest-growing

blocks.text: Alberta projects annual health-care spending growth of around four to five per cent, the report says, a range that "may be similarly realistic for other Canadian provinces given the ongoing demands on provincial health care systems."
New report suggests doctors haven't been freed up by virtual health care
Ultimately, Bartlett says, taxpayers won't measure the success of this hiring spree by headline job numbers, but by what happens when they actually seek care.
"When it comes to any public policy, what really matters to Canadians and taxpayers more broadly is that they see results for that public spending," he said.

"When you look at the hiring in the provinces that have increased spending the most, if that starts translating into better health-care outcomes … that should send a more positive signal to Canadians that some of the spending is going in the right direction."

articles.title: Jackdaw gasfield set to be approved by ministers this month, sources say
articles.summary: Energy secretary could recommend new North Sea drilling next week, as ministers also consider approval for Rosebank oilfield

blocks.text: Ministers are poised to approve a controversial new gasfield in the North Sea this month, according to government sources, and are considering approving a major oilfield later this year.

Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, will give her recommendation to approve the Jackdaw field off the coast of Aberdeen as soon as next week, according to people close to the decision, and the formal approval could follow a week after.
Meanwhile, officials are looking for ways to make sure any proceeds from the separate Rosebank project – if it is approved – go towards clean energy projects, as happens in Norway.
Officials have not yet finished their analysis of Rosebank’s environmental impact, but some close to the process believe they will soon decide the project should be approved.

Both projects have become emblematic of the government’s commitment to the North Sea, with green campaigners calling for them to be abandoned while the US president, Donald Trump, urges the prime minister to open them up.

A spokesperson for the energy department said: “The North Sea remains a vital national asset, supporting jobs, growth and the UK’s energy security. We are clear that oil and gas will continue to play an important role in our energy system for decades to come, alongside transitioning to clean power to protect jobs and tackle the climate crisis.”

Consultations on both Jackdaw and Rosebank, which the industry says will provide 10% of the UK’s oil and gas output at their peak, closed last month, since when Fahnbulleh has been considering her response.
Campaigners say the fields would produce as much as £336bn worth of damage to the economy as a result of the carbon pollution from the oil and gas that are produced.

Both fields have licences to operate, but environmental approval was rescinded after a judge ruled the companies running them – Shell and the Norwegian company Equinor – needed to account for the carbon emissions that would be produced by burning the oil and gas they produce.

The companies resubmitted their applications for environmental approval earlier this year. Granting those environmental permits would not violate Labour’s manifesto commitment not to issue new oil or gas licences, but many of the party’s MPs are opposed to the projects entirely.

Since he entered Downing Street, Andy Burnham has signalled he has concerns about the way in which the move to green energy has affected workers in the north east of Scotland, telling MPs this week: “I know that people have struggled with the impact of transition.”
Officials stress final decisions have not been made for either Jackdaw or Rosebank, but those close to the process say Fahnbulleh is likely to signal her approval for Jackdaw as soon as Monday.
after newsletter promotion

She will give her recommendation to the North Sea Transition Authority, which officials hope will issue the formal approval as soon as a week afterwards. Some in government think the NSTA process could take several weeks, however.

A decision on the £8.7bn Rosebank field, which is the biggest undeveloped field in UK waters and is estimated to contain as much as 500m barrels of oil or oil equivalent, is likely to come later in the year.

Fahnbulleh is likely approve that project if the environmental impact assessment allows it, according to sources, but is looking at ways to redirect the proceeds from it to clean energy projects in the UK. One option would be to put the tax revenues from the project into the national wealth fund, which has been set up to fund green energy schemes and other infrastructure projects.

Some in government warn this will be difficult, though, because the consenting process is already advanced and it could prove legally complex to change the terms on which the project is approved. The money has also already been accounted for in the Treasury’s forecasts, given the projects have their licences, meaning the chancellor, John Healey, would have to redirect it from other parts of government spending.

items: Robert Bolick is eager to represent the Philippines in the upcoming FIBA competition and Asian Games, expressing gratitude for the opportunity.
At 30 years old, Bolick is one of the elder statesmen on the national team, which includes several first-time players, and he aims to guide them while learning from their experiences.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – Robert Bolick is among the players fans believe deserve a spot on Gilas Pilipinas’ lineup for FIBA competition.

While his FIBA return has yet to come, Bolick is grateful for any opportunity to represent the country as he leads the team seeking to defend the Philippines’ throne in the Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, this September.

“I’m probably not the only one — everyone wants to be a part of it,” said Bolick in a mix of Filipino and English when asked about making the FIBA roster. “But at the same time, that’s not our decision to make. This is what’s given to us and we’re still honored to be part of this group.”
“I don’t know if it will happen, but if it does, of course, I’ll be happy.”
Bolick most notably donned the national colors in the 2019 FIBA World Cup in China, where he was the Philippines’ youngest player at 23 years old.
He finished the tournament as Gilas Pilipinas’ third-best scorer with 8.6 points behind Andray Blatche (15.8) and CJ Perez (12.6).
But his subsequent stints with the national team have been few and far between.

After Bolick saw action in a pair of games in 2022 in the Asian Qualifiers for the 2023 World Cup, it took him three years to make the national team again, helping the Philippines retain its title in the 2025 Southeast Asian Games in Thailand.

Now 30 years old and one of the elder statesmen, Bolick welcomes the chance to show the way for a national team that features multiple first-timers in Adrian Nocum, Sedrick Barefield, Jerrick Ahanmisi, Zavier Lucero, and Brandon Bates.

“I’m happy to see my fellow PBA players,” said the NLEX star. “I only get to see them play from a distance, and now, we’re all together. I’m happy that I’ll be able to learn from them, and hopefully, they’ll learn from me as well.”

Also composed of Don Trollano, RJ Abarrientos, Justine Baltazar, Justin Arana, Brandon Ganuelas-Rosser, and possibly, Justin Brownlee, the Nationals seek to become the first back-to-back Asian Games champion since China won in 2006 and 2010.

blocks.caption: Gilas ready for Asian Games defense with 11 players if Brownlee stays sidelined

blocks.text: While that is a tall order considering the level of playing field, Bolick believes the team can get the job done.
“My teammates here are all talented, so their expectation is to also win the gold. When we share the same mindset, it’s easier to accomplish that goal,” said Bolick.
Gilas Pilipinas opens its Asian Games title defense against Bahrain on September 11 before it battles Kazakhstan on September 12 and China on September 14. – Rappler.com

articles.title: South Korea pushes back on reports it is readying Hormuz deployment amid US pressure
articles.summary:
Seoul reportedly seeking parliamentary approval to send military assets to Middle East but president’s office plays down claims

South Korea is reviewing a possible deployment of military…

blocks.text: South Korea is reviewing a possible deployment of military assets to the strait of Hormuz amid pressure from Donald Trump over Seoul’s reluctance to provide support in the region, according to domestic media reports.

Citing unnamed government and military sources, the reportspublished on Thursday and Friday said preparations were under way and that the government intended to seek parliamentary approval for a new deployment. The reports, which appeared in major South Korean outlets, said the exact scale and timing have not been agreed.

But the presidential office pushed back, telling the Guardian that such reports were “different from the facts” and that “nothing related to the matter has been decided”, though it said the review was “continuing”.

An official said: “Our government has been closely discussing with the international community ways to make practical contributions for the speedy restoration of free navigation in the strait of Hormuz and peace and stability in the Middle East.”

According to reports, the assets under consideration include a P-8 Poseidon aircraft, which would mark South Korea’s first overseas deployment of a maritime patrol aircraft, and a naval logistics support ship to provide rear support.
One outlet, Seoul Broadcasting System, additionally reported that an explosive ordnance disposal team from the navy’s underwater demolition unit was part of the package.
Any new deployment in principle would require review by the national security council, a cabinet resolution and approval from the national assembly.
South Korea is highly dependent on the strait of Hormuz, importing more than 90% of its primary energy, including roughly 70% of crude oil through the waterway.

blocks.caption: The office of South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, said ‘nothing related to the matter has been decided’ in response to the media reports. Photograph: YONHAP/EPA

blocks.text: In 2020, the government of the then president Moon Jae-in expanded the mandate of an existing anti-piracy unit off the coast of Somalia to cover the strait of Hormuz, rather than seeking parliamentary approval for a new deployment.

South Korea’s defence minister, Ahn Gyu-back, in March told parliament that any deployment to the strait would require the national assembly’s consent given how different the mission would be from the unit’s existing anti-piracy mandate.

The reports come amid growing strains in the US-South Korea alliance. Trump has repeatedly complained in public that Seoul turned down his request for help over Iran, claiming in August that South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, had told him “No, thanks” despite the US stationing tens of thousands of troops on the peninsula.
Days later, he ordered the Ulchi Freedom Shield joint military exercises to be scaled back, shortening the drills by six days.

Relations between the two allies have also been strained by delays implementing a $350bn investment package Seoul agreed with Washington last year, reports that the US had restricted intelligence sharing with South Korea, and by a dispute over a data breach at the South Korean e-commerce company Coupang.
Separately, Seoul has expressed interest in taking part in any renewed US-North Korea diplomacy, as Trump signals openness to another meeting with Kim Jong-un.

articles.title: Malacañang on arrest warrant vs Sara Duterte: We respect the court's decision
articles.summary: Malacañang said Friday it respects the decision of the Quezon City (QC) court to issue an arrest warrant against Vice President Sara Duterte over her grave threats case.

blocks.text: Published September 4, 2026 3:46pm
Malacañang said Friday it respects the decision of the Quezon City (QC) court to issue an arrest warrant against Vice President Sara Duterte over her grave threats case.
“Ginagalang ng Palasyo ang anumang desision o kautusan ng korte,” Palace Press Officer Usec. Claire Castro said in a statement.
(The Palace respects any decision or order from the court.)

Atty. Paul Lawrence Lim, Duterte’s counsel for the grave threats cases filed by the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI), announced Friday afternoon that a Quezon City regional trial court has issued a warrant of arrest against the Vice President.
“Regardless of the question on jurisdiction, she has no intention of evading the law and will continue to exercise all her legal remedies,” Lim said.
A source in the Department of Justice (DOJ) also confirmed the information to GMA News.

In early August, the DOJ filed three counts of grave threats against the vice president over her remarks that she hired an individual to kill President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta Marcos, and former speaker Martin Romualdez, should an alleged plot against her succeed.
Prosecutors recommended the bail to be set at P120,000 per count.

Following this, Duterte filed a motion to quash on the ground of jurisdiction, arguing that she and other impeachable officers have limited procedural immunity while in office under the 1987 Constitution.
Duterte’s alleged grave threats against the President is also the basis of one of the Articles of Impeachment against her in the ongoing trial before the Senate impeachment court. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: Labour asks Met police to launch criminal inquiry into Reform UK donations after undercover report – UK politics live
articles.summary:
Two key aides to Nigel Farage have stepped down pending an internal investigation

Lee Anderson, the Reform UK chief whip and party chair, has said that James Orr and Dan…

blocks.text: Two aides suspended over donations allegations have 'no chance of coming back', says Reform UK's chair Lee Anderson

Lee Anderson, the Reform UK chief whip and party chair, has said that James Orr and Dan Jukes – the two aides primarily involved in the apparent plot exposed by an undercover investigation to evade electoral law – were suspended and won’t be coming back.
In an interview on Sky News this morning, Anderson said:
double quotation mark[Orr and Jukes] were told they had to step down. They have stepped down. And that’s got to be the right thing to do.

The presenter, Kamali Melbourne, put it to Anderson that Orr, head of policy at the party, and Jukes, a key aide to Nigel Farage, were both very important figures in the party and asked if there was any chance they could “come back”. Anderson replied:

double quotation markNo, there’s no chance of them coming back. They’ve stepped aside. We’re a serious party, you know, and sometimes in politics, you have to make tough decisions, harsh decisions. I think this probably was an easier decision, being given the option to stand down. They have gone. Like I said, they’ve left the building and our focus now is on the conference today.
Key events

items: nowAnderson says Farage won't quit over undercover report into donations, and 'country needs him'
16m agoTwo aides suspended over donations allegations have 'no chance of coming back', says Reform UK's chair Lee Anderson
28m agoFarage personally has 'serious questions to answer' over alleged Reform UK plot to evade electoral law, Ed Davey says
39m agoLabour asks Met police to launch criminal inquiry into Reform UK donations, as two party aides involved step down

blocks.text: Anderson says Farage won't quit over undercover report into donations, and 'country needs him'

In a separate interview, on Times Radio, Lee Anderson, the Reform UK chief whip and party chair, insisted there was no chance of Nigel Farage resigning over the undercover investigation into party donations.
Anderson said:

double quotation markI don’t think Nigel has got any questions on this. The two people involved, they have gone. They have left the building. I keep saying this time and time again. They have gone. That is the right thing to do. They are not coming back and Nigel is going nowhere … Nigel is an honest man. I have known him for many years now. The party has done the right thing by launching this investigation. Nigel will be on the main stage later on explaining our first 100 days in government. He is not going anywhere. The country needs him.

While James Orr and Dan Jukes are the main focus of the investigation, the film shown by Channel 4 News suggests Farage himself also had some knowledge of the proposal for a US-based supporter to donate £500,000 to the party by channelling it through his UK-based son. Foreigners are not allowed to donate to UK political parties, and donating via proxies in this manner is also banned.
Farage is filmed attending an oyster bar lunch where he thought he was meeting the father and son. But the ‘son’ was an undercover reporter, and the ‘father’ an actor hired to play the part.
After discussion of how the money from the UK might be given to the party via the son, Farage is recorded telling them: “Thank you both.”
Farage personally has 'serious questions to answer' over alleged Reform UK plot to evade electoral law, Ed Davey says

Ed Davey, the Lib Dem leader, says Nigel Farage was ultimately responsible for the apparent attempt to evade electoral law on donations exposed by the undercover investigation shown on Channel 4 News.
In a post on social media this morning, he says:
double quotation markSo much for this being a “hoax” then. Clearly very serious questions for Farage to answer given his role in the meeting. The buck stops with him.

Davey was referring to the way Reform UK, in its first response to the undercover report last night, said it had “been the target of a hoax perpetuated by foreign-funded, climate change activists posing as would-be party donors”.
Labour asks Met police to launch criminal inquiry into Reform UK donations, as two party aides involved step down

Good morning. Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, is speaking on the main day of his party’s conference in Birmingham. It has been a bad summer for the party. After having a large lead over the other parties in opinion polls for over a year, the lead collapsed after Andy Burnham became PM, and now Reform UK and Labour are basically neck and neck. Farage has been embroiled in the scandal over his failure to declare a £5m donation. And last night, on the eve of Farage’s big speech, Channel 4 News broadcast the findings of a long, undercover investigation showing leading Reform UK figures apparently plotting to evade UK law on electoral donations.
Here is Rowena Mason’s story.
You can read the Channel 4 News write-up here. But to fully appreciate how strong the evidence against Reform UK is, it is best to watch the half-hour report in full.
There are two developments this morning.

items: Reform UK says the two senior Reform officials most implicated in the apparent plot to evade electoral law are stepping down pending an investigation. In a statement released about half an hour ago, a Reform UK spokesperson said:

blocks.text: double quotation markReform UK has launched an investigation following the broadcast of a Channel 4 News programme. Both individuals involved have stepped down from their respective positions pending the outcome of the investigation. The party believes it is important that the investigation is allowed to proceed independently and without prejudice. No further comment will be made while the investigation is ongoing.
This is a reference to James Orr, the party’s head of policy, and Dan Jukes, a senior aide to Farage.

items: The Labour party has written to the Metropolitan police calling for a criminal investigation. In her letter to Mark Rowley, the Met commissioner, Bridget Phillipson, the Labour party chair, says:

blocks.text: double quotation markWe … believe there is a proper basis for a police investigation into whether offences under PPERA [Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000] have been committed, including, but not necessarily limited to: (a) offences under section 61(1) concerning evasion of restrictions on donations; (b) any offence arising from knowingly providing false information to, or withholding material information from, the registered treasurer in circumstances falling within section 61(2); (c) any offence arising from Reform UK’s acceptance or retention of impermissible donations, including the £32,500 of polling expenditure, if the evidential and reporting facts establish the necessary elements; and (d) any related offence concerning the accuracy or completeness of statutory donation returns. We understand that political finance matters also fall within the regulatory remit of the Electoral Commission. We are not suggesting that a police investigation should displace the commission’s role; rather, given the apparent possibility of criminal conduct, we believe the allegations should be brought formally to the attention of the police so that the appropriate authorities can determine the proper investigative route.
Here is the agenda for the day.

11.05am: The main day of Reform UK’s conference opens with tributes to Ann Widdecombe. After that the main speakers on the stage are chief whip Lee Anderson at 11.30am; Welsh leader Dan Thomas at 11.45am; home affairs spokesperson Zia Yusuf at noon; Jordon Bardella, president of the French National Rally party at 12.30pm: Matt Goodwin at 3pm; Sarah Pochin MP at 3.15pm; deputy leader Richard Tice at 3.30pm: and Nigel Farage at 3.50pm. There are also fringe meetings through the day.
1pm: Farage and Bardella hold a press conference.
Afternoon: Kemi Badenoch is on a visit in West Sussex.

I will be blogging until around lunchtime, and then colleagues will be taking over. I’m afraid we are no longer able to have comments open below the line every day on this blog. If you want to contact us, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this email to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints.

articles.title: Fact check: Barzaga's post falsely claims 'floodwater' being 'recycled' in Marikina flood control
articles.summary: The payloader in Marikina was cleaning mud, not “recycling” floodwater for flood control, contrary to a viral claim.

blocks.text: September 4, 2026 | 3:44pm
A payloader scoops and returns water to an area in Marikina City, prompting claims that "floodwater" was being “recycled” for flood control.
Screenshot / Marikina River Water Level
MANILA, Philippines — A viral post claiming that “floodwater” was being scooped up and returned to the same area, or “recycled,” as part of flood control efforts in Marikina City is false.
MP MIKO POGAY questioned why a payloader was returning water in Marikina, while Kiko Barzaga sarcastically criticized the act.
Screenshot taken Sept. 4, 2026, 1:25 p.m.

In an August 30 post, Facebook user MP MIKO POGAY questioned why the loader was returning the “floodwater” it had collected to the area, calling what he claimed was a “flood control” effort a “water transfer challenge.”
The post's caption said, in part:
From baha, back to baha. Zero waste! RECYCLE YARN?! ??????????
Expelled lawmaker Kiko Barzaga also posted the video on his page, sarcastically praising Marikina’s flood control.
“Lipat na ako diyan sa 2028,” he joked.
Rating: This is false.
Facts

The Facebook posts incorrectly characterized the loader returning water to what appears to be a flooded area as a flood control effort amid continuous rains and heavy flooding from recent storms and the southwest monsoon or habagat.
Both posts included less than 15 seconds of the three-minute video, leaving out the portion that provides context on what the payloader was being used for.
Marikina River Water Level posted the full video showing the payloader being used to clean and remove mud.
In the full video posted by Facebook page Marikina River Water Level, the person recording said the payloader was being used to clean and remove mud.
“Habang inaayos pa ang motor, ito muna ang ginagamit para panglinis at matanggal ang putik,” the person said. Earlier in the video, the person said the motor was being used for flushing operations.

The Marikina River reached the second alarm at 9 a.m. on August 30, when the video was taken, according to the caption of the Marikina River Water Level post and an update from the Marikina Public Information Office (PIO).

The city's local government unit deployed skid loaders, heavy equipment, and clearing personnel to remove garbage, mud, and debris left behind by the floods in Malanday, Tumana, and Nangka, according to the Marikina PIO on August 30.
MMDA General Manager Nicolas Torre III explained that water was being used to clean the payloader’s bucket.
Metropolitan Manila Development Authority (MMDA) General Manager Nicolas Torre III also explained that the payloader was cleaning its bucket.

"At para two-in-one ang trabaho, ’yung tubig na ginagamit na panlinis ng bucket, ibinubuhos din sa gilid para tangayin ang burak at mga latak na naiwan pagkatapos ng baha," Torre said on August 31 in a Facebook post, tagging Barzaga and vlogger Boss Dada.
Torre also addressed Barzaga directly, saying that not all water seen in the area was floodwater: “Meow, hindi lahat ng nakikita mong tubig ay baha.”
Why we fact-checked this

At least 8.8 million people have been affected by Tropical Cyclones Luis, Maymay, Neneng and the habagat, with 33 reported deaths, the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council (NDRRMC) said on August 31.
Around 2.5 million families across 10 regions had been affected, with about 164,500 people staying in 1,365 evacuation centers nationwide, according to the NDRRMC.
MP MIKO POGAY's post has garnered at least 80,000 reactions, 8,500 comments, and 5,000 shares. Meanwhile, Barzaga's reel has gained more than 126,000 reactions, 100 comments, and 5,300 shares.

articles.title: Meloni government becomes longest-serving in postwar Italy
articles.summary: The hard-right government has officially beaten the record set by media tycoon Silvio Berlusconi. Meloni and her party are using the opportunity to celebrate and also rally for the 2027 election.

image.caption: Meloni and her far-right Brothers of Italy (Fdl) party are planning a celebration on Friday evening in the port city of Bari [FILE: Jul 20, 2026]Image: Stefano Costantino/Avalon/Photoshot/picture alliance

blocks.text: The right-wing government of Giorgia Meloni on Friday became the longest-serving since the Italian Republic was established 80 years ago.
Meloni's government, the most-right wing to have ruled Italy since World War II, has been in charge for 1,413 days.

That's one day more than billionaire media tycoon Silvio Berlusconi, who still holds the record for collectively serving longest as prime minister with nine years in office, albeit under different governments.
Since Italy became a republic after the end of the war, it has had 68 governments within 80 years, with governments lasting around 13 months on average.
How is Meloni celebrating her record tenure?
Meloni and her far-right Brothers of Italy (Fdl) party are planning a celebration on Friday in the port city of Bari in the southern Puglia region.
Some 80 coaches will transport supporters there, with Meloni due to address the gathering in the evening.
Deputy Prime Ministers Matteo Salvini and Antonio Tajani are also due to appear via video link. The event is effectively an opportunity to campaign for Italy's 2027 election.
What does the Meloni government and its supporters say?
The Meloni government boasts one million extra people in employment in its four years in power, unemployment below 6% as well as a €21 billion ($24 billion) reduction in personal income taxes.
They are also especially proud of what they say is a sharp decline in migrant arrivals.
The prime minister, whose party has neo-Fascist roots, also says Italy's influence on the world stage has grown.

Meloni's nationalist streak was celebrated at home on more than one occasion. One notable example was when US President Donald Trump, with whom the Italian leader had initially and unusually enjoyed a cordial relationship, said she had begged him for a photo.
"Italy doesn't beg," Meloni said of Trump's claim, much to the satisfaction of many Italians.
Trump-Meloni feud escalating
What do Meloni's critics say?
Critics of Italy's first female prime minister and her longest-serving government however argue that despite the numbers, the country's persistent problems remain.
They list weak productivity, demographic decline and long-standing inefficiencies in healthcare, education and public administration. The rising cost of living is also a major criticism.

"Have wages increased? No. Petrol costs more, job insecurity has increased, people are retiring less and the healthcare system is functioning less effectively," Maurizio Landini, head of the CGIL trade union, said ahead of the celebrations.
Italian unions strike to protest new budget priorities

Parallel to the Meloni party in Bari, her opponents are also planning a gathering across the city. Organizers accuse her government of creating a "war and weapons economy" and a "police state," as well as fueling a climate of hate against migrants.
Meanwhile, others think the prime minister strayed from her election campaign and has become too moderate, including a potential challenger in the coming vote.
Retired army general Roberto Vannacci, whose party is further to the far right than Meloni's, is known for hard-line positions on immigration and national identity.
Polls show his party has overtaken both the anti-immigrant League and right-wing Forza Italia parties, both members of Meloni's ruling coalition.

articles.title: PNP studying possible amendments to SIM Registration Law
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine National Police (PNP) on Friday said it was studying possible amendments to Republic Act No. 11934 or the Subscriber Identity Module (SIM) Registration Law. “The…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine National Police (PNP) on Friday said it was studying possible amendments to Republic Act No. 11934 or the Subscriber Identity Module (SIM) Registration Law.

“The PNP is ready to provide its insights and data that will push for the amendment of the law, making it more effective when it comes to crime prevention,” the agency’s chief, Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr., said in a statement.
“I have directed our legal team to look into this and make the necessary recommendations,” he noted.

The top cop’s instruction came after concerns raised by the Anti-Cybercrime Group (ACG) about frequent arrests of individuals allegedly selling pre-registered SIM cards and the possibility that pre-registered SIM cards are being used in cybercrimes.
The ACG made this pronouncement last week, while detailing the arrest of a 26-year-old man in Obando, Bulacan, for the alleged illegal sale of 400 pre-registered SIM cards.

“Innovations in digital technology are fast evolving, and we really need to keep up [with] more efficient and effective approaches in running after illegal activities and eventually make cyberspace safe for every Filipino,” Nartatez explained./coa

articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) is considering filing an ethics complaint against Batangas Rep. Leandro Leviste before the House of Representatives next week,…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) is considering filing an ethics complaint against Batangas Rep. Leandro Leviste before the House of Representatives next week, Director Melvin Matibag said on Friday.

Matibag said this after announcing that the bureau will file on Friday afternoon “qualified human trafficking” charges against the congressman and six others after completing its investigation into the supposed “honey trap” plot against Executive Secretary Ralph Recto.
“Next week we will be considering also filing […] a case to the ethics committee of the House of Representatives against Congressman Leandro Leviste,” Matibag noted in an ambush interview on Friday.
The NBI director said he does not know Leviste’s exact current location but noted that he is “definitely still out of the country.”
“Last time that we monitored him, he was in France; hindi ko lang alam ngayon kung nasaan na siya,” he said.
(Last time that we monitored him, he was in France; I just don’t know where he is now.)
The Inquirer reached out to Leviste regarding the matter, but he has yet to respond as of this writing.
Last August 6, Matibag and the Bureau of Immigration confirmed in separate statements that Leviste and his mother, Sen. Loren Legarda, have left the country through separate flights on August 2.
Leviste was implicated by a nabbed talent manager—Alias Ken—as the alleged “financer” in the “honey trap plot” against Recto.

Aside from Leviste, Negros Oriental Rep. Jacinto “Jing” Paras, alias Ken, and four lawyers from the Rondain and Mendiola Law Firm who were supposedly tasked to create fabricated statements against Recto were implicated.
The congressman and other implicated individuals have since denied Alias Ken’s allegations of a supposed plot against the executive secretary./coa

articles.title: DENR eyes monitoring system for endangered Samar Rafflesia flower
articles.summary: TACLOBAN CITY — The Department of Environment and Natural Resources – Samar Island Natural Park (DENR-SINP) is developing a Biodiversity Monitoring System (BMS) to conserve the endangered Samar…

blocks.text: TACLOBAN CITY — The Department of Environment and Natural Resources – Samar Island Natural Park (DENR-SINP) is developing a Biodiversity Monitoring System (BMS) to conserve the endangered Samar Rafflesia (Rafflesia manillana) in Basey, Samar.
The initiative follows the rediscovery and documentation of the rare flowering plant in Sitio Bagong Silang, Barangay Guirang in Basey town, about 15 years after it was last recorded there.
DENR is also collaborating with experts on further research about the specie.

The Protected Area Management Office (PAMO) – SINP said in a statement on Friday that the monitoring system will provide a more systematic way to track the rare plant, its habitat and potential threats to its survival.

“The DENR-SINP also plans to work with experts to generate additional scientific information that could guide conservation measures for the specie, including its habitat requirements and relationship with its host vine,” the agency stated.
A DENR-SINP team documented 24 visible buds and flowers, including one fully bloomed flower, during surveys conducted in the upland area of Guirang village on May 26-28 and June 9-11.
According to available records, the site is currently the only confirmed location of Rafflesia manillana.

“The 2026 documentation is significant because it confirms that Rafflesia manillana continues to survive in its natural habitat after approximately 15 years without a known documented record,” the DENR-SINP added.
The Samar Rafflesia is endemic to Samar and is classified as endangered under DENR Administrative Order 2026-20.
To complement scientific monitoring, the PAMO-SINP, in partnership with Basey’s local government unit, recently conducted a communication, education, and public awareness campaign.
The activity is meant to encourage residents to help protect the specie and its habitat.
Residents were briefed on the ecological importance and conservation status of the Rafflesia, and its dependence on a specific forest habitat and host vine.
DENR officials said disturbing surrounding vegetation could threaten the plant’s survival.
The awareness campaign highlighted threat indicators near the Rafflesia habitat, such as signs of illegal timber poaching and human activities that could cause forest degradation.
Residents were encouraged to report activities that could threaten the Rafflesia and its habitat.

Experts also discussed Republic Act 11038, or the Expanded National Integrated Protected Areas System Act of 2018, which prohibits unauthorized activities that may damage protected habitats and wildlife.

The DENR-SINP emphasized that ongoing monitoring, research and collaboration with conservation experts and local communities are crucial for creating long-term measures to protect the Samar Rafflesia. /apl

articles.title: How Volkswagen's huge workforce became a costly burden
articles.summary: The struggling German carmaker plans to cut up to 100,000 jobs from its 630,000-strong workforce. How did VW's headcount get so bloated, and will the cuts be enough to survive the Chinese EV…

image.caption: VW has 60% more employees than Toyota, which makes a similar number of carsImage: Moritz Frankenberg/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Volkswagen has built one of the largest workforces in the global auto industry.
At nearly 630,000 people — 680,000 if you count joint ventures in China — VW employs around 60% more workers than Toyota, 140% more than Stellantis and nearly 240% more than Ford.

That headcount was once a sign of Germany's industrial might and VW's huge profits. Now, it's become a massive burden, one that's forcing the company to make painful job cuts to survive against agile Chinese competitors.

After already trimming thousands of positions last year as profits came under pressure, Volkswagen is now preparing to slash 50,000 additional jobs worldwide, including tens of thousands in Germany. The proposal got the backing of the VW Supervisory Board on Thursday, September 2.
VW also wants to close four German factories, a plan that the supervisory board on Thursday stopped short of agreeing to implement right away.

These cuts include VW luxury brands like Porsche and Audi. Other German automakers and suppliers are facing similar pressures. Mercedes-Benz is planning to cut several thousand jobs, and suppliers like Bosch have announced large cost savings.
How VW got to this point
Much of VW's headcount issue stems from long-standing strategic decisions.

Meghan Ostertag, an analyst for economic policy at the US-based Information Technology and Innovation Foundation, says VW's much larger workforce was needed because the firm chose to control more stages of production than its peers.

"The company makes many of its components and software internally, increasing the demand for labor and, of course, labor costs," Ostertag told DW, adding that factory expenses in Germany can be "up to twice those of the competition."
Other experts point to an aggressive acquisition strategy over the years, which brought brands including Skoda, Porsche, SEAT and Bugatti into the VW fold — not to mention several truck makers.

"That strategy worked to some extent, but the complexities of integrating all those brands, supply chains and different designs make VW very complicated to operate," Daniel Harrison, senior automotive analyst at the London-based Ultima Media, told DW.
Can Volkswagen's 'legacy' help restore its former glory?
Why the VW model broke
Although Volkswagen survived the 2015 Dieselgate emissions scandal without suffering lasting financial damage, the company incurred massive costs and soon faced a new set of problems.

The company was slow to transition its production to electric vehicles (EVs) — just as Chinese EV makers gained serious traction and a technological edge. That delay contributed to slower sales in China, which accounted for a third of total VW sales, as well as softening demand in Europe and other key markets.

VW also repeated a mistake made by the US auto industry decades earlier. In the 1960s and 1970s, the Big Three — Ford, GM, and Chrysler (now part of Stellantis) — were bloated and slow to adapt when Japanese and European competitors began eating into their market share.
By the time US carmakers shifted toward leaner production methods, a decade had passed, and they had fallen significantly behind, noted Ostertag.
Toyota, which produces a similar number of vehicles as VW, operates with nearly half the workers by relying more on suppliers, higher automation, and a simpler management structure.

blocks.caption: Four German plants, including this one at Zwickau, are facing closureImage: AAPimages/Wehnert/picture alliance

blocks.text: In a research note, auto industry analyst Matthias Schmidt pointed to another factor: the "stranglehold" that trade unions and a key shareholder have over VW. This, he said, had helped cause "years of neglect in readjusting workforce numbers."

The northern German state of Lower Saxony — home to Volkswagen's global headquarters in Wolfsburg — holds 20% of voting rights in the company, can veto major decisions, and has previously pressured executives not to close plants or lay off staff, notably during the Dieselgate and COVID supply chain crises. It's ramping up the pressure this time, too.
Over the decades, Germany's powerful unions, meanwhile, have repeatedly held out for high wage increases and generous benefits, which have made VW staff among the best-paid autoworkers in the world.

blocks.caption: With plants in Thailand and Brazil, China's BYD opening a factory in HungaryImage: Jin Haoyuan/Xinhua/IMAGO

blocks.text: Is VW's turnaround plan enough?
Analysts warn that the company may have to cut more than the annual €4 billion the firm hopes to save to secure its future.

The current proposals to cut 50,000 additional jobs, they say, will bring savings and help improve short-term profitability. But VW's underlying cost base and slow decision-making culture mean deeper, more radical reforms may well be needed.

VW should "invest more heavily in automation," Ostertag told DW, adding that it would allow the carmaker to "better compete with leaner firms," such as China's BYD, one of the fastest-growing EV brands in Europe.

Analysts say VW has lagged peers in plant automation levels but has stepped up investments in robotics and digital upgrades for its EV production. The company is also planning its first sub-€20,000 EV next year.

With China responsible for around 30% of VW's global vehicle output, Harrison predicts more production shifts to Asia and the potential to share VW's European plants with Chinese EV producers, a move previously seen as "unthinkable."
Chinese EV maker BYD goes Europe
German government, EU offer a lifeline
On the policy front, the German government is providing subsidies and loans for domestic EV battery plants to help cut reliance on Chinese imports.

The European Union, meanwhile, is advancing the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA). The IAA is meant to boost the bloc's competitiveness and shield strategic industries from unfair competition from China.
The EU has already imposed tariffs of up to 45% on Chinese-made EVs. But they are far below the 100% levies that the US charges, which have largely shut Chinese competitors out of the US auto market.
Historian Niall Ferguson from Harvard University warned that Europe has been slow to respond to China's strategy of giving huge subsidies to EV makers that help undercut European rivals.
"Unless there's radical change, I predict: Europeans will be driving Chinese cars on a massive scale very soon," Ferguson told Germany's Süddeutsche Zeitung newspaper earlier this year.

During the same interview, economist Moritz Schularick, President of the Kiel Institute for the World Economy, suggested using market access as leverage — only allowing Chinese brands to sell in Europe if they produce locally.
Schularick responded provocatively when questioned on VW's long-term future, predicting that Germany's auto giant would "likely be bought by a Chinese car maker like BYD."
Editor's note: The article, originally published on July 7, 2026, has been updated to include the VW Supervisory Board's backing for a restructuring plan calling for an additional 50,000 job cuts.
