articles.title: Volkswagen board approves plan to cut another 50,000 jobs
articles.summary: The group - which includes Audi, Porsche, Skoda as well as the VW brand - plans to cut a total of 100,000 by 2030.

blocks.text: The board of German car giant Volkswagen has approved a plan to cut another 50,000 jobs as part of a sweeping turnaround programme. It brings the total number of roles the company plans to shed by 2030 to 100,000.
The group - which includes Audi, Porsche, Skoda as well as the VW brand - said in March that it would cut 50,000 roles by the end of the decade.
The move is a "strong signal" for the future of the firm, which is "taking responsibility for our entire workforce", VW's chief executive Oliver Blume said in a statement on Thursday.
Blume said in July that the firm was looking to make the additional cuts.
The Beetle-maker has been hit by a drop in profits due to falling sales and fierce competition, especially from Chinese brands.
VW will also prioritise the "most compelling vehicles" and make more of each model, which will help lower costs, it said.
A "fundamental adjustment of the global workforce capability is necessary" to safeguard the competitiveness of the company, which faces shifting demand and technological change.
It added "a Group-wide workforce adjustment of approximately 50,000 positions - including management roles - will be necessary."
The company is also considering the future of its Emden, Zwickau, Hanover and Neckarsulm plants, where it has said production capacity exceeds demand.
"Alternative uses for these plants are being assessed," it said.
The restructuring marks the biggest in VW's almost nine-decade history.
As of 2025, VW employed more than 660,000 people worldwide. Its brands also include Seat, Bentley and Lamborghini.

Christianne Benner - the president of Europe's largest industrial union IG Metall and deputy chair of VW's Supervisory Board - said the carmaker had "fought hard for good solutions" to address a "crisis situation".
VW's profits have fallen sharply in recent years, hit by falling sales in China, which was once one of its biggest markets.
Sales have also fallen in the US, partly due to the impact of tariffs on car imports that were introduced by President Donald Trump's administration.
Chinese carmakers have been expanding aggressively as they roll out new technologies while benefiting from lower production costs than their rivals.
In recent years, firms like BYD have seen their sales rise sharply in markets including the UK, European Union and South East Asia.

articles.title: Missouri state legislative candidate accused of trying to plant cocaine on opponent
articles.summary:
Republican candidate Thomas Ross and his former campaign manager devised a plan to stash drugs in their opponent Louise Secker’s purse or vehicle

A Missouri House race has been rocked by the…

blocks.text: A Missouri House race has been rocked by the Wednesday arrest of Republican candidate Thomas Ross, whom prosecutors accuse of attempting to frame his primary opponent Louise Secker for cocaine possession.

In June, Ross allegedly gave his former campaign manager, identified by the initials “CS” in court documents, a bag of cocaine and Adderall. The two devised a plan for the former manager to stash the drugs in Secker’s purse or vehicle.
On 21 June, Ross asked for an update on the plot.
“Taking it no luck with the substance of it all?” he wrote in a text to his staffer. “Substance” was a euphemism for the narcotics, authorities say.

“I am actually creeping down to the car show right now and seeing if I can see your car. I have had it on me for a couple days in order to be able to take full advantage of any opportunity that arises,” the former manager replied, according to court documents.
“I thought I had it at the forum Walter went to, but never got close [and] car was locked.”

The Joplin police department in Missouri alerted the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) on 30 July to a public corruption matter. (It’s unclear how the police were alerted to the alleged scheme.) The next day, the federal agency gave the former manager a covert recording device, which he used to tape a conversation with Ross.
The former manager offered to call in an anonymous tip about Secker’s car containing drugs and asked if Ross wanted it done.
“If you can pull it off … pull it off,” Ross replied.
Ross has been charged with conspiring to distribute a controlled substance. It’s unclear if the former manager will also face criminal charges.
Secker did not immediately respond to a phone call.

Ross defeated Secker in August by a razor-thin margin of just 33 votes in the Republican primary for House District 161. The district includes Joplin, a city about 70 miles (112 km) west of Springfield.
The incumbent state representative, Republican Lane Roberts, is not running for reelection.
Missouri Republican party chair Peter Kinder called on Ross to withdraw from the race.

“While Mr. Ross is entitled to due process and the facts surrounding this matter must be allowed to come to light, the circumstances of his arrest are serious and deeply troubling,” Kinder said in a statement.
“The people of the 161st District deserve a nominee who can devote his full attention to earning their trust and representing their interests in Jefferson City.”

articles.title: Canadians should prepare for a 5 C hotter future, report warns
articles.summary: The federal government's new report summarizing the latest science on climate change warns that under current climate policies, the impact on Canadians will likely be "far from benign."

image.caption: A woman bikes along the waterfront in Toronto as wildfire smoke fills the city in July. A report from the federal government suggests that under current global climate policies, Canadians should expect fire season to continue to lengthen. (Laura Proctor/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New
The federal government's new report summarizing the latest science on climate change warns that under current climate policies, the impact on Canadians will likely be "far from benign."
In Nunavut, warming in winter could exceed 10 C
Canadians will have to prepare for a future that's 5 C hotter, according to a new report summarizing the latest science on climate change.

The second edition of Canada's Changing Climate Report, a synthesis of the science on the impact of a warming planet on Canadians, confirms with greater confidence that burning fossil fuels, or what the report calls "human activities," are responsible for climate change.
On Thursday, the federal government released a summary of the report's findings.
The report is forward-looking, assessing what Canada would look like under different scenarios depending on whether countries fulfil their climate commitments.

"We do still have some agency," said Nathan Gillett, one of the report's authors and a research scientist with Environment and Climate Change Canada. "Where emissions go from here will affect how temperatures evolve through the century and whether we can stabilize temperature or whether it just keeps increasing."

items: Carney government asks court to strike down climate litigation
These may be the UN climate panel's last words before we hit 1.5 C limit

blocks.text: The report finds that if global governments keep pursuing their current climate policies, Canada will still see intensified warming, which "corresponds to a future climate for Canada that is far from benign," the report states.
Glaciers could 'largely disappear'
Under such a scenario, Canada is projected to warm through this century with an estimated temperature increase of 5 C. In Nunavut, warming in winter could exceed 10 C.

Glaciers in western Canada are projected to lose more than 75 per cent of their ice, it finds, and there's a more than 60 per cent likelihood that the central Arctic Ocean will be ice-free most Septembers.
"Iconic landscapes are changing across Canada as snow and ice disappear," the report states. "Glaciers in western Canada will largely disappear by the end of this century."
Satellite images show glacier collapse that triggered flooding at Nepal-China border
Beyond considerable warming in the North, the report paints a difficult future in southern Canada, where most of the country lives.
Summer droughts are projected to become longer, more intense, and more frequent in central and southern Canada, the report states.
Canadians should also brace for an increase in the frequency and intensity of flash flooding and atmospheric rivers.

items: Climate change made Canadian wildfires in N.W.T. and Ontario roughly twice as likely, analysis finds
Is Canada flunking climate? The picture isn’t great, but there might be a way out

blocks.text: "Multiple lines of evidence support the finding that the length of the fire season has increased in most parts of Canada and is projected to continue to lengthen as global temperature rises," the report states.
Things would look even worse for Canada if countries abandoned their climate policies, with average temperatures projected to increase 6.9 C this century.
If the world, however, dramatically reduces greenhouse gases and achieves net-zero around 2075, Canada's climate is projected to stabilize and average warming would increase by 3.5 C.
Report is 'physics, not fate'

Despite the grim picture the report paints, 5 C of warming is not locked in, and there's still time for Canada to avoid a hotter future, independent policy research organization the Canadian Climate Institute says.
"This report describes physics, not fate," the group said in a statement.
Cutting emissions in Canada and around the globe, the institute says, will determine "whether Canadians have to live with the consequences of more than 5 C of warming or 3.5 C."

The institute says each degree of warming that's avoided will save lives and prevent homes, communities and livelihoods from being destroyed. It will also save the Canadian economy billions of dollars, the statement says.
In a statement responding to the federal report, a climate advocacy group called for greater action to reduce emissions, linking Toronto's flash flooding on Wednesday to climate change.

"As the climate breakdown accelerates, more than 65,000 Torontonians lost power in yesterday's severe storm, often for many hours," said Toronto city Coun. Dianne Saxe, writing for Climate Caucus, a network of municipal leaders from across the country. "There was also extensive disruption to traffic and to transit, and expensive flood and wind damage to homes."
"Our communities cannot afford the frequent human and economic blows that oil and gas use are causing."
Responding to the report, a statement from Canada's environment minister said Canada remains committed to reducing its emissions and achieving net-zero by 2050.

"Our government is moving with urgency to fight climate change, while working together to build the energy security, industrial capacity, and strategic autonomy that will define this century for Canada," said Chris Zhou, the director of communications for the environment and climate change minister.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

David Thurton is a senior reporter in CBC's Parliamentary Bureau. He covers daily politics in the nation’s capital and specializes in environment and energy policy. Born in Canada but raised in Trinidad and Tobago, he’s moved around more times than he can count. He’s worked for CBC in several provinces and territories, including Alberta and the Northwest Territories. He can be reached at david.thurton@cbc.ca

articles.summary: The jury now faces a seventh day of deliberations in the triple-murder trial.

blocks.text: The jury in the Lindsay Clancy case failed to reach a verdict on their sixth day of deliberations.
Clancy's lawyer asked the judge to remove a juror after the jury forewoman sent a court note saying one holdout would not follow the court's instructions on reasonable doubt.
The defence's request to remove the juror was denied by the judge.
The BBC's Ana Faguy breaks down how the dramatic day in court unfolded.

articles.title: Tensions flare as judge declines to remove juror in Lindsay Clancy trial
articles.summary: The defence lawyer is upset after the judge decides not to remove a holdout in the triple murder case.

blocks.text: A judge has again told the deadlocked jury in Lindsay Clancy's murder trial to keep trying to reach a verdict after a dramatic sixth day of deliberations in a case that has gripped America.
Tensions flared in court after the jury forewoman sent the judge a note saying one juror would not follow the judge's instructions on reasonable doubt.
There was audible shock in the room when the defence team asked for the juror to be removed, a request that was denied by the judge.

Clancy, 36, is charged with three counts of first-degree murder in the deaths of her three children - Cora, five, Dawson, three, and eight-month-old Callan - at her Massachusetts family home on 24 January 2023.
Warning: This article contains distressing details
The former labour and delivery nurse does not deny strangling her two sons and daughter in the basement of their house.
But her lawyer argues she was suffering from postpartum psychosis at the time, and could not distinguish right from wrong.
The jury of nine women and three men in Plymouth has deliberated for some 35 hours without a verdict, following nearly six weeks of trial proceedings.
The panel has twice previously sent the judge notes saying it could not come to a unanimous decision, but Thursday was the first hint of rancour in the deliberation room.

Clancy's lawyer, Kevin Reddington, said in court that the jury forewoman had sent another note, this one complaining to Judge William Sullivan that a juror was refusing to listen to the law on reasonable doubt.
Reddington and prosecutor Jennifer Sprague had an animated discussion with the judge in court.
Reporters in the room could not hear the exchange, but the BBC saw exasperated facial expressions and gestures from Clancy's lawyer.
Reddington then went over to Clancy to explain what had just happened, in what seemed to be a tense conversation.
Clancy, who was paralysed from the waist down when she jumped out of a second-floor window after killing her children, was pushed in her wheelchair by her lawyer to join a discussion with the judge.
Afterwards, Judge Sullivan brought in each juror individually and questioned them.

He reminded the panel they must unanimously believe beyond reasonable doubt that the defendant is guilty in order to convict her of a crime. As each juror came up, some looked at Clancy, while others did not.
When the defence lawyer told the court about his request to have a juror removed, there were gasps and reporters quickly began typing.
Clancy bowed her head as the media begin to exit the room.
Reddington, looking upset, could be seen consoling his client, holding her in a side hug and rubbing her back as journalists left court.

The defence lawyer told reporters afterwards that the forewoman's note to the judge stated that there was one holdout in the jury who, as he described it, "refuses to listen to the law... on reasonable doubt".
Reddington said he had suggested to the judge "a motion to remove the juror who refuses to accept your instructions on the law on a reasonable doubt".
The defence lawyer said he had no indication of what this lone juror was thinking and he did not confirm the 11-1 split the jury forewoman reported earlier.
The issue with the juror is expected to be addressed again when court convenes at 09:00 EST (14:00 BST) on Friday.
If the jury does not reach a verdict and Judge Sullivan declares a mistrial, prosecutors would need to decide whether to retry the case.
Clancy faces life in prison without parole if convicted of first-degree murder.
If found not guilty by reason of lack of criminal responsibility, or reason of insanity, she could be committed to a state psychiatric hospital.
Under US law, a jury must unanimously believe "beyond a reasonable doubt" that someone is guilty in order to convict them of a crime.
The designation is the strictest standard in the US legal system. It places the burden on the government to prove that the accused is guilty, and not the accused to prove their innocence.

If you are suffering distress or despair and need support, you could speak to a health professional, or an organisation that offers support. Details of help available in many countries can be found at Befrienders Worldwide. www.befrienders.org.
In the UK a list of organisations that can help is available at bbc.co.uk/actionline.

articles.title: U.S. aims 'to really tighten the screws' on Cuba with newest sanctions: analyst
articles.summary: The U.S. government on Thursday slapped new sanctions on Cuba in a fresh push to strangle the island's economy and deepen its multiple crises.

image.caption: A man pulls a cart carrying drinking water along a street in Havana last month. On Thursday, the U.S. government slapped new sanctions on Cuba in a fresh push to strangle the island's economy and deepen its multiple crises. (Ramon Espinosa/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New
The U.S. government on Thursday slapped new sanctions on Cuba in a fresh push to strangle the island's economy and deepen its multiple crises.
Company that imports parts needed to maintain Cuba's power grid among those hit with sanctions

Among those hit with sanctions are Fidel Ernesto Castro, grandson of former president Raúl Castro, and Cuba's Oil Industry Supply Import Co., known as Abapet. The company is responsible for importing special equipment and spare parts needed to sustain Cuba's crumbling power grid.

The sanctions aim to push Cuba's critical machinery offline and exacerbate its energy crisis, said Brett Erickson, a sanctions expert and managing principal at Obsidian Risk Advisors, a consulting firm.
"The U.S. is trying to really tighten the screws as much as possible," he said.

"The Trump administration seems to have no seriousness to accept any change from Cuba other than a toppling of regime. Marco is not going to let that go," he added, referring to U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
Erickson anticipated that Cuba's government would try to circumvent the sanctions "because they have to."
"They'll get creative in how they try to procure these maintenance parts," he said, warning it would be a costlier alternative, which in turn would raise inflation and further hurt Cuba's economy.
Frequent outages, fuel reserves dwindling

Islandwide blackouts have become increasingly common, while daily outages in Cuba now surpass 24 hours as the aging grid fails and fuel reserves dwindle ever since U.S. President Donald Trump in late January threatened tariffs on any country that sells or provides oil to the island.

"The goal in theory is to create so much civilian hardship and suffering that they have no option but to essentially rise up and topple their government," Erickson said. "It is an attempt to cause a humanitarian crisis."
Talks earlier this year between the U.S. and Cuba have since halted, while sanctions have increased in recent months.

Erickson said he expects the U.S. to keep targeting smaller and smaller state companies to try to push them "into a death spiral." The U.S. has previously sanctioned entities including Cuba's state-owned oil and gas company.
LISTEN | Cuba and fears of a U.S. invasion:
Front Burner32:39Will the U.S. invade Cuba?
The U.S. State Department made the announcement just hours after Cuban officials held a press conference to share more details on the historic economic reforms approved in June.
When asked about the current situation in Cuba, Oscar Pérez-Oliva Fraga, Cuba's deputy prime minister and minister of foreign investment, blamed the U.S. government.
"This past year has been very complex, and we know why," he said. "The blockade is a genocide."
He spoke before the sanctions were announced.
No sense of 'what's going to happen to you'

Among the Cubans exhausted by the ongoing outages is 49-year-old Yaqueline Bernal. She said Thursday that she hasn't had electricity since Sunday and worries most about the consequences for her eight young grandchildren.
"If we don't have power, we don't have water," she said. "You really don't know what's going to happen to you."
Bruno Rodríguez, Cuba's foreign affairs minister, decried the latest sanctions on X.

"Collective punishment is a crime. So, too, is inflicting suffering on an entire population through measures coldly calculated to trigger a humanitarian crisis," he said. "Enough with the abuse. Put an end to the blockade once and for all and allow Cuba to live in peace."
Eugenio Martínez Enríquez, Cuba's ambassador in Mexico, called Rubio "a liar without scruples."
"We will not forget his crimes," he wrote on X.
Meanwhile, Rubio asserted on X that those sanctioned "are part of the corrupt Castro financial and intelligence network."

"Cuba's Communist regime elites preside over a failed state where ordinary Cubans go hungry while the Castro family and other insiders enrich themselves through sanctions evasion and other illicit schemes — and seek to export subversive Marxist ideology to the United States and other states in the Western Hemisphere," he wrote.
"Trump and I are unwavering in our commitment that Cuba will be free."

articles.title: 8 years on, Philippines yet to claim Filipino seafarer's remains from Somalia
articles.summary: The Department of Foreign Affairs has vowed to send fresh instructions to the Philippine embassy in Nairobi, Kenya, to press Somali authorities to return the remains of a Filipino seafarer who died…

blocks.text: September 4, 2026 | 8:49am
Rep. Brian Poe Llamanzares (FPJ Panday Bayanihan party-list) addresses Department of Foreign Affairs officials during a budget hearing at the House of Representatives on Thursday, Sept. 3, 2026.
Llamanzares' office via FB

MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Foreign Affairs has vowed to send fresh instructions to the Philippine embassy in Nairobi, Kenya, to press Somali authorities to return the remains of a Filipino seafarer who died more than eight years ago, after its latest request went unanswered.

Sam Dela Cruz, a 25-year-old seafarer registered with manning agency GMM Global Maritime, died of cardiopulmonary arrest in Somalia on July 28, 2018. His remains have yet to be brought back to the Philippines.

The issue was brought up during Thursday's House deliberations on the DFA's proposed 2027 budget, when Rep. Brian Poe Llamanzares (FPJ Panday Bayanihan), vice chair of the House appropriations committee, asked the department what progress had been made to repatriate Dela Cruz' remains.
The DFA said its attempts since 2018 to return Dela Cruz' remains have stalled in the absence of a Philippine mission in Somalia and the COVID-19 pandemic.
Dela Cruz' burial was carried out immediately under Somalia's Islamic Sharia law before the family could weigh in.

Context reported in 2025 that a burial request was filed with a Somali court the day after Dela Cruz's death. The agency he was under, GMM Global maritime, no longer appears in a Singapore online business directory, "which can mean it has ceased operations or changed names," the report stated.

"We understand the immense difficulty and emotional pain the family continues to endure during this prolonged process," Undersecretary Ezzedin Tago, DFA's officer in charge of migrant affairs told House lawmakers. "The DFA remains committed to supporting the Dela Cruz family."
Because the Philippines has no mission in Somalia, the case has been handled through the Philippine embassy in Nairobi, which holds jurisdiction over the country.
The DFA official said the embassy has a record of diplomatic notes sent to the Somali government since 2018, none of which drew an official reply.
GMM Global Maritime reached out to Somali authorities in November 2018 and located Dela Cruz's burial site in Bosaso, roughly 1,000 kilometers from the capital, Mogadishu, according to the DFA.
The manning agency secured permits and funding for exhumation and reached a "preliminary agreement with local officials," but negotiations stalled and the exhumation never happened.

In 2025, the DFA asked the Nairobi embassy to raise the case again with the Somali embassy there, to relay the department's and family's request to the Somalian government. That, too, went unanswered, Tago said.
"With that update, we will reinstruct or send the instructions again to our embassy in Nairobi to meet with the Somali embassy in Nairobi to revive this issue," the DFA official said.
Poa said Somalia's non-response was "not our fault," but said the government should continue to "try its best to bring home the body of our kababayan."
"We should not stop knocking at their door to ask for the body back," Poe said.

articles.title: Kenya's chai tea lovers are not happy as the nation's cows run dry
articles.summary: Supermarket shelves are emptying, sellers are rationing supplies and prices are rising.

blocks.text: Kenya's chai tea lovers are not happy as the nation's cows run dry
Image source, Getty Images
Chai, made by boiling tea in generous amounts of milk, is sometimes flavoured with ginger and spices
ByBasillioh Rukanga
Reporting fromNairobi
Kenyans love their milky tea, or chai, but some are facing the worrying possibility of doing without as the country has been hit by a milk shortage.

A breakfast here is often incomplete without a cup of chai, made by boiling tea in generous amounts of milk, sometimes flavoured with ginger and spices. It is often served at meetings and during social visits, with many people taking the hot brew several times a day.
But now some may have to do without as supermarket chilled sections are nearly empty. Retailers have upped the price and are limiting how much shoppers can take home.
The government has put the dearth of milk in recent months down to drought, which has significantly reduced pasture and hampered production.
But the recent shortages are unusual, with the country's industry regulator itself admitting to "supply constraints" and "low stock levels" across the country.
Muthoni Macharia, who runs a restaurant in the capital, Nairobi, usually buys more than 70 packets of fresh milk - and is desperate and puzzled by the scarcity.
"Where has the milk gone?" she asked when the BBC spoke to her as she was out searching for at least a few packets to quench her customers thirst for chai.

blocks.caption: Image caption, For restaurant owner Muthoni Macharia, the milk shortage means a loss of business

blocks.text: For restaurant owner Muthoni Macharia, the milk shortage means a loss of business
Macharia says there have been shortages for about a week - and it was especially affecting her morning rush hour. Her regulars are not happy: some opting to take their tea black - but many will not.
"If they come in groups, and there's no milk tea, you see that's a loss for me," she said.
Kenya is one of the leading milk producers on the continent.

A long-established commercial dairy industry has led to pasteurised milk being very popular, particularly in urban areas, with Kenyans ranked among Africa's highest consumers, according to industry data.
Raw and fermented milk is more widely drunk in rural areas.
The milk shortage has sparked widespread public concern with some people promoting unfounded conspiracy theories about supermarkets deliberately trying to profit.

According to the Kenya Dairy Board (KDB), the government body that oversees the dairy sector, formal milk deliveries to processors fell by 3.7% from 84.4 million litres in June to 81.3 million litres in July, while preliminary investigations suggest deliveries declined further in August.
The Consumer Federation of Kenya (Cofek) says there has been a downward trend of supply since the beginning of the year.
It attributes this to a delay in the seasonal rains, which has reduced the grazing ground available, coupled with a 45% rise in the cost of animal feed.
Cofek has expressed concern over the rationing as well as the increasing cost, saying fresh milk prices have risen from 70 to 80 Kenyan shillings ($0.54 to $0.62; £0.40 to £0.46) a litre.
"This shortage was foreseeable, and in material part, avoidable," it says.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Normally fresh milk is in plentiful supply on supermarket shelves

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
Normally fresh milk is in plentiful supply on supermarket shelves

The consumer body says dairy processor New KCC, a state-owned company, and the KDB did not adequately absorb the milk surplus last year, adding that powder processed from the excess milk would have helped resolve the current crisis.
Some of the milk processors in Kenya often reconvert the powder into the more-preferred liquid milk during dry seasons when the supply of fresh milk goes down.
"Had these buffers been in place, today's supply shock would have been substantially cushioned," Cofek says.
It has demanded a recovery plan to include fodder and subsidy support for farmers.
This would include waiving of taxes on animal feed inputs, as well as "active retail price monitoring to deter opportunity price gouging and rationing".
In response to media enquiries, the dairy board's managing director William Maritim assured that despite the "temporary supply constraint", milk continued to be available.
Fresh pasteurised milk, which has a shorter shelf life, had been more affected than the more long-life UHT milk, he said.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Dairy cows need to eat well to produce milk

blocks.text: Dairy cows need to eat well to produce milk
Customers at Nairobi supermarkets on the hunt for milk told the BBC they were worried about rising costs.

"Sometimes when I go to the supermarket I find there is none. When I do find some, the price has gone up. Today it is this price, tomorrow it has gone up again," said Bernard Abok, who does his shopping after finishing work.
Patricia Gathoni said if the prices kept going up she would have to rethink what she gave her children, saying she had resorted to adding water to the milk that she managed to buy.

On Thursday, agriculture ministry officials held a meeting with the association of dairy processors about the problem, with the ministry committing to support farmers, stabilise milk supply and protect consumers.
The ministry's top official in charge of livestock development, Jonathan Mueke, said the immediate focus was to get more feed for farmers, including through duty-free importation of yellow maize.
He said they were also looking at longer-term solutions that would manage stability across periods when there was surplus milk and when there were shortages.

Reports of milk going to waste are not uncommon during periods of a dairy glut. Farmers have often complained about how little they are paid for their perishable produce at such times - but they have few options because of limited processing or storage capacity.
According to Mueke, the government is considering setting up a fund to help support the preservation of milk during such periods.
In the meantime, the government is also considering temporarily importing milk from the neighbouring countries to ease the shortage.
For the devoted Kenyan chai lover, that may offer some respite.

articles.title: Global Affairs collecting DNA from families of Canadians missing in Nepal
articles.summary: Federal government officials said Global Affairs Canada is working to collect DNA from the families of Canadians still missing in Nepal and China after a flash flood ripped through the border region…

image.caption: An aerial view shows houses standing amid debris during a helicopter flight from Nuwakot to Rasuwa following the deadly flash floods and mudslides in Nepal. Officials are searching for hundreds of missing people, including 29 Canadians. (Navesh Chitrakar/Reuters)

blocks.text: Canada

Federal government officials said Global Affairs Canada is working to collect DNA from the families of Canadians still missing in Nepal and China after a flash flood ripped through the border region last week.
There are 29 Canadians unaccounted for following flash flooding last week

Senior government officials, briefing reporters on background, said they are starting to collect the samples from the families of 29 people still considered missing, with assistance from the RCMP and police forces in Nepal and China.
The flooding on Aug. 26 killed more than 1,100 people and left roughly 4,400 missing after a glacier collapsed in the Himalayan border region between Nepal and China.
In Kathmandu, police have buried dozens of unidentified bodies in trenches because there are too many to keep or identify individually.
Canadian located safe
One Canadian was found safe, while the remaining 29 are believed to have been in the region where the flash flood occurred.
The Nepal Tourism Board reported on Sept. 1 that more than 580 foreign nationals and tourists were still unaccounted for, while another 330 had been rescued.
Federal officials said the situation is changing by the day and they continue to work with local authorities and the families of the missing.
Global Affairs has 10 officials in Kathmandu and has established points of contact with the families of the missing Canadians.
Search, recovery and identification efforts are being led by Nepali and Chinese authorities and Canada has offered assistance, the federal officials said.

articles.title: Girl group Katseye are missing two members, but their tour still dazzles
articles.summary: Reduced but resilient, girl group Katseye received a hero's welcome in London.

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Only two-thirds of the girl band made it to London, but fans seemed thrilled nonetheless (L-R: Megan, Yoonchae, Lara and Daniela)
They may have been two members down, but the pop group Katseye received a hero's welcome as they played their first full concert in the UK.
The audience erupted with screams even before the show began, as the band broadcast their music videos on the O2 Arena's big screens, and the noise barely dipped for the next three hours.

It was proof that Katseye have become pop's biggest property (they're currently the most-streamed act on YouTube UK) even while singers Manon Bannerman and Sophia Laforteza are on health-related hiatus.
The stage felt emptier without them, but their bandmates worked hard to fill the gaps, hyping up the crowd with a succession of bass-heavy pop anthems and jaw-dropping dance breaks.

"Are you happy to see us?" asked the band's youngest member, Yoonchae Jeong, as if the answer hadn't been obvious from the moment they appeared in a storm of laser lights and launched into the Brazilian funk workout of Hootie Frutti.
"I think you guys are our loudest crowd ever, literally," marvelled Megan Skiendiel.
"This crowd is unbelievable," added Lara Raj.
The concert was only the second date of the band's Wildworld tour - but fans already knew every twist and turn from social media.
There was even a cheer of relief when Daniela Avanzini survived a complicated lift in the dance routine for Gabriella. On the opening night, her dance partner dropped her., external

blocks.caption: Image caption, Daniela recovered from her stage fall in Dublin with no injuries.

blocks.text: Image source, Katseye / Hybe / UMG
Daniela recovered from her stage fall in Dublin with no injuries.
Such adulation - and scrutiny - has come quickly for Katseye.
Based in Los Angeles, the multinational girl group were only formed in 2023 as part of the online reality competition show The Debut: Dream Academy.

The contest was created by Hybe, the South Korean entertainment company behind acts like BTS and Le Sserafim, and the US record label Geffen, home to Olivia Rodrigo and the Rolling Stones. Of the 120,000 who initially applied for the show, only six made it through.

Trained under the rigorous K-Pop system, they had a breakout year in 2025, first with the hyperactive electro-skronk of their single Gnarly, then with its follow-up, a slinky ballad called Gabriela that highlighted Daniella's Cuban-Venezuelan roots.
In London, their audience skewed young: The queue for pick and mix was longer than the one for the bar.
When Megan asked, "Whose first concert is this?" the air curdled with screams.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The group’s first world tour is scheduled to run until the end of the year.

blocks.text: The group’s first world tour is scheduled to run until the end of the year.
Throughout the show, fans shook lightsticks, parroted Katseye's dance moves and, in some cases, spontaneously burst into tears.
Many concert-goers also wore bindis, inspired by Lara, who has proudly incorporated her Asian heritage into her aesthetic.
One individual also came dressed as a courgette, a reference to Internet Girl's so-weird-it-almost-works refrain, "Eat zucchini".
The energy was infectious. And, if you looked closely, the parents were enjoying the show as much as their kids.
Even Spice Girl Melanie C is a fan, hosting a Q&A with the band during their first UK trip last October.
"They're incredible girls," she told the BBC earlier this summer. "They've got great music, they've got a great work ethic, and they're really beautiful, you know?
"Obviously, they've had a little drama, as happens with all bands, but they work so goddamn hard."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Sophia Laforteza, officially the band's leader, said she needed to take a break from the band's gruelling schedule

blocks.text: Sophia Laforteza, officially the band's leader, said she needed to take a break from the band's gruelling schedule
The drama began in February, when Manon announced she was taking a hiatus from the band to "focus on her health and wellbeing".

It came after the Swiss-Ghanaian singer told BBC News the band had been subject to racism and death threats; but fans also highlighted Katseye's gruelling schedule, suggesting they were being overworked.
In April, she posted a message to fans saying she was having "positive conversations" with Katseye's management, but not before she removed references to the band from her Instagram biography.
Then, just months after Manon stepped back, Sophia announced she was also going on hiatus to protect her "mental health and wellness".
"You can't pour from an empty cup," she posted on social media. "It's important to care for yourself."

blocks.caption: Image caption, The group were nominated for best new artist at the 2026 Grammys (L-R): Yoonchae, Megan, Lara, Manon, Sophia and Daniella

blocks.text: The group were nominated for best new artist at the 2026 Grammys (L-R): Yoonchae, Megan, Lara, Manon, Sophia and Daniella
Although it was hoped Sophia would return for the European leg of the Wildworld tour, that's proved impossible.
Her mother assured fans the absence is only temporary.
"Don't worry, this is for her own good," she told ABS-CBN News, external. "This is what I love about her management. They realise when the girls are tired.
"It's a good thing that she is resting so that she's stronger when she comes back."
It is not unusual for members of K-Pop bands to take a break when the mental or physical demands of the job become overwhelming.

Lia from the girl group Itzy took more than a year off work to seek treatment for "extreme levels of anxiety" in 2023-24; while Moka, a singer from Katseye's labelmates Illit, is currently on extended hiatus, also for anxiety.
In keeping with K-Pop tradition, Katseye honoured Sophia's place in the band during Tuesday's show, retaining her pre-recorded vocals on songs like Mean Girls and Pinky Up.
Manon's lyrics, however, were sung by other members of the band - presumably because her hiatus pre-dated production and rehearsals
Vocal criticisms
Which brings me to a related point. After the tour's opened in Dublin on Tuesday, Katseye were accused of miming throughout their set.
But from what I could tell on Thursday, the member's microphones were live all night, with a backing track doubling their vocals at crucial moments.
On slower songs like Tonight I Might and My Way they proved more than capable as live performers.

Meanwhile, Lara's vocals on the solo showcase unloveu (proudly introduced as "the first Katseye song written by a member of Katseye") mixed power and emotion in a way that suggested the band have potential beyond the ear candy pop that's become their trademark.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Katseye will play a second night in London, before heading to Manchester and then to Europe

blocks.text: Katseye will play a second night in London, before heading to Manchester and then to Europe
Other highlights included Daniela's death-defying dance break, complete with aerial splits, that led into Gabriella; and Megan's technotronic shakedown at the end of Pinky Up.

For Yoonchae, the show's high point was Time Lapse, where she got to sing in her native Korean, while mingling with the crowd. ("Keep your hands to yourselves and don't throw any gifts on the stage for our safety," warned Lara, spoiling the atmosphere just a little).
The show ended on a powerful note, with Iconic By Mistake - the band's defiant response to an online hate campaign - and an extended romp through Gnarly, complete with a leather-studded rock remix.
All told, it was a stunningly confident and self-assured show from a band who could easily been diminished by personnel problems.
"This is not a goodbye," promised Yooncahe as Katseye waved goodbye. "We'll come back."
Glastonbury's Pyramid Stage would be a perfect fit.

articles.title: Trump names Adam Telle as acting army secretary following the departure of Driscoll
articles.summary:
Telle has previously worked for Trump during his first term as a special assistant to the president for legislative affairs

Donald Trump on Thursday named Adam Telle as the acting army…

blocks.text: Donald Trump on Thursday named Adam Telle as the acting army secretary after the departure of Daniel Driscoll amid widespread reports of tensions with defense secretary Pete Hegseth.
Telle is currently the assistant secretary of the army for civil works.
“He is a Great Patriot, who is respected by all,” the US president wrote in a Truth Social post.

Driscoll gave no explanation for his decision to quit this week as the army’s top civilian official. His clashes with Hegseth have been widely reported, and some of Driscoll’s allies in the army were ousted this year by Trump’s Pentagon chief.

Telle has been at the Army Office of Civil Works since August 2025, according to Legistorm, a website that tracks lawmakers and Capitol Hill staffers. Before that, Telle spent 20 years mostly working in Congress for lawmakers, including as chief of staff for Republican Senator Bill Hagerty of Tennessee from 2021 to 2025.

Telle had a job for 18 months working in the White House during Trump’s first term as a special assistant to the president for legislative affairs, Legistorm said. He also spent more than 10 years working for the late Republican Senator Thad Cochran of Mississippi.
Telle will be overseeing the country’s largest fighting force at a time when the US is still engaged in conflict with Iran and significant army forces are stationed in the Middle East.

The war has significantly contributed to the US military’s shortfall in critical weapons like the Patriot and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (Thaad) missile interceptor systems, which are operated by the army.
Driscoll, an army veteran who served in Iraq, did not offer an explanation for why he stepped down after 18 months as the service’s civilian leader.

He is a friend of vice-president JD Vance and had good relationships with both Republicans and Democrats in Congress. His allies in the army who were ousted by Hegseth included its top uniformed leader, Gen Randy George.
Gen Christopher LaNeve took over as the army’s acting chief of staff and recently pulled the plug on a drone modernization program that Driscoll had championed.
Driscoll spoke with Trump on the current state of the army before he submitted his resignation, the Associated Press has reported.
Driscoll did not allude to any problems in the only public statement on his departure, saying Tuesday that it has been “the honor of a lifetime” to serve as army secretary under Trump and Hegseth.
“We could not have made the progress we did without the support of secretary Hegseth,” he added.
Democrats and Republicans lamented Driscoll’s departure, with some blaming Hegseth directly.
Sen Thom Tillis, a North Carolina Republican who is retiring and sometimes has clashed with Trump, said on social media that Hegseth “is creating a leadership void at the top of our military ranks”.

articles.title: Split verdict in New Orleans murder trial tied to staged-wrecks scheme
articles.summary:
Sean Alfortish and Leon Parker convicted on some counts but not murder charges linked to insurance fraud plot

A federal jury in New Orleans on Thursday returned a split verdict after more…

blocks.text: A federal jury in New Orleans on Thursday returned a split verdict after more than 30 hours of deliberations in a three-week-long blockbuster fraud and murder trial that garnered headlines far beyond Louisiana.

Jurors deadlocked on murder charges Sean Alfortish and Leon “Chunky” Parker faced, leading US district judge Wendy Vitter to declare a mistrial as prosecutors vowed to try the case on those counts again.

“Today’s verdict is an important step towards justice,” US attorney David Courcelle of the eastern district of Louisiana said at a Thursday press conference. “Alfortish and Parker exploited the courts to benefit themselves and confederates.”

Alfortish was found guilty of conspiracy to commit mail and wire fraud, two counts of mail fraud, obstruction of justice, and witness tampering. He was found not guilty of another count of obstruction of justice and subornation of perjury.

Jurors were not able to reach verdicts on charges Alfortish and Parker faced of conspiracy to commit witness tampering through murder, witness tampering through murder, conspiracy to retaliate against a witness through murder, retaliation against a witness through murder and causing death through use of a firearm.
That means the jury was not able to reach a unanimous verdict.
Vitter declared a mistrial on the five murder-related counts against Alfortish and Parker.
Alfortish faces 90 years in prison. Parker, who previously pleaded guilty to conspiracy and two counts of mail fraud, faces up to 60 years.

Dubbed “Operation Sideswipe”, more than 63 people have previously been convicted in the massive scheme that involved so-called “slammers” who would get into accidents with 18-wheelers to file fraudulent insurance claims.
The unresolved charges center on the killing of Cornelius Garrison, who prosecutors said was cooperating with the FBI in its investigation into the staged-crash scheme.

Prosecutors accused Alfortish and Parker of conspiring to kill Garrison in the front door of his mother’s home after learning he was talking to federal investigators. Prosecutors also alleged Alfortish paid Parker to carry out the killing.

“They brought every resource of the federal government that they could bring. They brought five assistant US attorneys on to the case. They had a phalanx of FBI agents. They tried in every way possible to convict Sean Alfortish of murdering a federal informant. And the jury did not find in their favor,” Shaune Clarke, Alforitsh’s attorney, told reporters after the verdict.
“They couldn’t prove it this time. And they’re not going to be able to prove it the next time because it isn’t true. It didn’t happen.”

“We’re appreciative of the jury refusing to convict on this evidence, which we think was an appropriate decision, and I’ll leave it at that,” Stephen Haedicke, Parker’s attorney, said on the courthouse steps.

articles.title: Volkswagen to cut 100,000 jobs by end of decade
articles.summary: The company will carry out the biggest job cuts ever seen in the industry. Volkswagen also plans to restructure and invest in research.

image.caption: Volkswagen's Zwickau plant is expected to be affected by the cuts [FILE: June 2026]Image: Hendrik Schmidt/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: German automobile giant Volkswagenannounced on Thursday that it would be cutting a total of 100,000 jobs by the end of the decade in what is set to be the biggest restructuring ever seen in the global car industry.
The company said that management and trade unions had approved a plan involving the reduction of a further 50,000 jobs, in addition to 50,000 redundancies already agreed.
"It is essential to systematically align workforce levels with economic realities," read a statement from the multi-brand Volkswagen group which, apart from VW itself, also includes Audiand Porsche.
The total of 100,000 cuts amount to about 15% of Volkswagen staff worldwide. The cull eclipses the 50,000 job cuts General Motors made after it declared bankruptcy in 2009.

Unions and management had publicly rowed before signing off on the plans, with the former accusing the latter of not been honest with the workforce after the figure of 100,000 possible job cuts surfaced in the media before being communicated internally.
'The motor of the entire region'

What's more, Volkswagen also said the long-term future of four major German plants – in Hannover, Emden, Zwickau and Neckarsulm — could not be guaranteed. Their closure would mark the first full-scale shuttering of Volkswagen factories in its home country.
"If this plant really were shut down, you could put a big black spot on the map," one long-term employee in Zwickau, Saxony, told the AFP news agency.
"The plant and the jobs outside it, our suppliers, they're the motor of the entire region."
Caught between US tariffs, Chinese competition and a sluggish growth in demand for electric vehicles, Europe's largest carmaker is in trouble.
Company reforms to drive profitability
However, CEO Oliver Blume insisted that the decision to cut 100,000 jobs sent "a strong signal for the future of the Volkswagen Group."

blocks.caption: Volkswagen CEO Oliver Blume said that the company will take responsibility for its entire workforce, its partners, and industrial jobs worldwide [FILE: March 2026]Image: Julian Stratenschulte/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Volkswagen did not give details as to the timing of the cuts and how they would be distributed across the different regions where it has plants and offices, but the company said its focus will turn to North America and that it is looking to expand exports to the Global South.
The plan also includes a three-digit-billion sum investment over the coming years as VW looks to improve technologically through research and development and become more competitive.
Among the moves is a structural change that should bring about faster decision-making and a cut to the number of businesses and holdings it owns by about one-third.

articles.title: High-profile VPD officer and youth charity CEO Kal Dosanjh charged with theft, fraud
articles.summary: Vancouver police officer, anti-gang advocate and youth charity CEO Kal Dosanjh has been charged with theft, fraud and breach of trust offences dating back to 2017.

image.caption: A file photo of Vancouver Police officer Kal Dosanjh in 2018. He has been charged with multiple instances of fraud over $5,000. (Doug Kerr/CBC)

blocks.text: British Columbia·Updated
Vancouver police officer, anti-gang advocate and youth charity CEO Kal Dosanjh has been charged with theft, fraud and breach of trust offences dating back to 2017.
Alleged offences go back as far as 2017
Dosanjh was arrested and taken into custody on Thursday.
A charge document reveals he is facing multiple counts of fraud over $5,000, and theft over $5,000.
According to the document sworn on Thursday, multiple charges relate to alleged fraud and stealing from investors of multiple property development projects.
Those include the Azura, Queen's Park and Sahara development projects.
The alleged offences occurred between Jan. 13, 2017, and Oct. 31, 2024, according to the document, with Sarabjit Singh Gill listed as a co-defendant.
According to B.C. Supreme Court documents, the two men are listed as partners in multiple property development ventures, which have been the subject of multiple civil lawsuits.
The two have denied all wrongdoing in those cases.
Dosanjh also faces two charges alleging he committed fraud over $5,000 and stole from the KidsPlay Youth Foundation, the charity that he founded in 2015.
Those alleged crimes occurred between Dec. 8, 2017, and July 25, 2025, according to the document.
Dosanjh also faces one count of breach of trust by a public officer.
On Thursday afternoon, plain-clothes and uniformed VPD officers were seen carrying boxes out of a home listed as Dosanjh's residence in court documents.
Dosanjh has been a VPD employee for more than two decades.
In 2015, he founded the KidsPlay Youth Foundation, a charity with the stated aim of "keeping B.C. kids away from a life of crime."
Dosanjh has made multiple media appearances in his role as the charity's CEO, with the non-profit often organizing sports events in a bid to engage youth with community programs.

items: Vancouver police officer charged with 1 count of assault

blocks.text: Alliance Lawyers in Langley, a law firm representing Dosanjh, sent CBC News a statement saying it was "inappropriate to draw conclusions" based on the reported arrest of their client.
"Mr. Dosanjh has committed no crime and is innocent of any wrongdoing," the statement reads.
"An arrest, or a report that an arrest has occurred, is not evidence of guilt, misconduct, or criminal responsibility."
With files from Jason Proctor and Akshay Kulkarni

articles.title: Venezuelans of all stripes are denouncing Trump's 'biggest oil deal ever'
articles.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump's oil deal with interim Venezuelan President Delcy Rodriguez is being rejected by the Venezuelan opposition, and by some in her own party. Venezuelan Canadians, some with…

image.caption: U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright and Venezuelan interim President Delcy Rodriguez shake hands at Miraflores Palace in Caracas, Venezuela, on Wednesday. (Leonardo Fernandez Viloria/Reuters)

blocks.text: Venezuela's opposition leader Maria Corina Machado broke several days of silence on Thursday with a video statement in which she rejected the oil deal signed on Wednesday in Caracas between the U.S. government and Venezuela's interim president, Delcy Rodriguez.

"I understand what you are feeling," she told her compatriots, "sadness, anger and that painful feeling so familiar throughout our history of someone else making decisions about what belongs to us, in our name, without asking us."
Machado's statement came a day after both Trump and Rodriguez refused to offer any schedule for a return to democracy in Venezuela, and Trump again praised the Rodriguez government.
"We are very happy with the president-elect that we have right now, the people that are running it," Trump said on Tuesday. (Rodriguez has not, in fact, been elected to the post.)
Trump announces deal to control vast amount of Venezuelan oil reserves

While she had always believed Venezuela's oil industry needed U.S. investment to recover, Machado said, Rodriguez's government had no legitimacy to make such a deal, which needed to wait for the return of democracy and rule of law.
She also said there was confusion about the real terms of the deal. Many Venezuelans share that confusion, but already know they don't like it.

Neither U.S. President Donald Trump and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio's social media posts, nor a White House statement, nor Rodriguez's speech clarified exactly how or when 17 Venezuelan oilfields would be rejuvenated and start producing the 65 billion barrels covered by Trump's "biggest oil deal ever."
Extracting oil over releasing prisoners
Many Venezuelan Canadians, including some with deep knowledge of the country's oil industry, have reacted negatively to the announcement.

"It's frustration, disappointment and rage," said Rebecca Sarfatti of Toronto, co-founder of the Canada Venezuela Democracy Forum. "We were used as a country, as an oil power, to get whatever Trump wanted. And Miss Delcy is playing the game so she can stay in power."
Sarfatti says Venezuelans are exasperated by the eagerness to get at Venezuela's resources and the relative lack of interest in liberating political prisoners.

Lino Carrillo, former general manager of operations for Nexen Energy in Fort McMurray, Alta., and a veteran of both Venezuela's and Canada's oil industries, is a member of Machado's advisory group on oil and energy.

"Anybody that signs with Delcy will be exposed to transparency in the end," he told CBC News. "When a new government comes in, they're going to review everything that has been signed by Delcy, by Trump or any U.S. government, or any European government for that matter."
"What they're doing is against the constitution of Venezuela."

Venezuelans have grown increasingly skeptical of U.S. motivations in their country since the Jan. 3 capture of Nicolas Maduro, he said: "There is an old saying that you judge people for what they do and not for what they say."

The announcement by Trump only sharpened Venezuelans' frustration at the fact that eight months after the U.S. seized Maduro in the raid on Caracas, the dictatorship he led has been allowed to remain in power, while Trump describes its unelected leader as "highly respected."

Among Republican politicians in Florida, there were growing signs of unease with the closeness of the Trump administration to the rump chavista dictatorship that has become its partner in Venezuela. Florida Republicans complained about the lack of movement toward democracy and expressed support for Machado, repeatedly scorned by the Trump administration.

The deal also appeared to split Delcy Rodriguez's own party. Prominent chavista congresswoman Iris Varela put out a video statement saying the deal was signed "under duress" and vowing to repudiate it as soon as Trump leaves office.
Even some of the most enthusiastic "MAGAzuelans," the Venezuelans who most put their trust in Trump and criticized anyone who disagreed, appeared to be rethinking their assessments.
Controversial figure at the centre of the deal

Venezuelan criticisms of the deal focus on the fact that it was negotiated secretly with an illegitimate government, through a Venezuelan intermediary seen in the country as a classic example of the bolichico class — a businessman who has profited through his connections to the chavista regime.
A fact sheet published by the White House on Monday night described an unusual joint venture between the Pentagon and a private company called North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP).

items: Trump's Venezuelan oil deal: What we know and how it could impact Canada's oil industry
The U.S. could soon control 20% of Venezuela's oil reserves. Canada's oilpatch isn't worried
Chevron expands Venezuela presence with $7B US plan

blocks.text: The U.S. State Department would have a right to 20 per cent of production "at cost," and right of first refusal on the remaining 80 per cent. Venezuela would be guaranteed $19 US per barrel in royalties, regardless of the price of oil.

NABEP was formed out of Blue Energy, a company run by Florida oil and asphalt magnate Harry Sargeant III, a Trump golf partner and major GOP donor who did a lot of business with the Maduro regime (Maduro once called him "the only gringo I trust.")
But Sargeant sold his stake to Venezuelan businessman Alejandro Betancourt, who has been investigated for allegedly laundering embezzled Venezuelan money in several countries, but never charged.
Rubio defended Betancourt's involvement by saying he is not suspected of wrongdoing on U.S. territory, as U.S. media reported Trump administration pressure campaigns to drop European investigations.
A 'highly irregular' deal
Venezuelan Canadians in the oil industry have no illusions about the state of the industry they were forced to leave behind.
Jorge Robles, who spent his career in Venezuelan and Albertan oilfields, says people understand that Venezuela needs foreign investment and that it has to give something in return.
"I was prepared to have negotiations that were very uncomfortable and disadvantageous to Venezuela," he told CBC News.
But he said there was something "highly irregular" about the way this deal was negotiated.
"The U.S. is there negotiating on behalf of the Venezuelan reserve, but to offer that to companies that belong to the United States. So it's an obvious conflict of interest," he said.
Robles said it was "really upsetting and concerning" that the administration is focusing on oil, rather than political prisoners.
He said he fears that any money Venezuela receives will merely be used by the chavista regime to further entrench itself.
Midterm voters may be true target

But the two oilmen also say that given the deal's cold reception in Venezuela, oil companies are unlikely to want to bet on its long-term survival, or on a country where the situation remains so uncertain.

"If we don't get to a situation where there is a due process in Venezuela, freedom and people can walk on the street without fear, then don't expect any company to send people to Venezuela," said Robles.
They both said the announced deal appeared to be partly about convincing American voters in the run-up to the midterms that high gas prices will soon start dropping.
What could massive U.S. and Venezuelan oil deal mean for Alberta?

"It's just a lot of noise to try to influence votes in the States," said Carrillo, adding that the price of oil will respond far more to any reopening in the Strait of Hormuz than far-off plans for oil investment in the Orinoco Basin.
"The markets are not dumb," he said. "The markets are watching that."

Carrillo said he intends to return to Venezuela to offer his expertise to put the devastated oil industry back on its feet, but won't do so unless there is a deal ratified by a democratic Venezuelan government.
Fears of creeping colonization

Many Venezuelans have expressed fears of a creeping colonization of their country, in which the chavista dictatorship is maintained in power by the Trump administration as a subcontractor of its control.

"I do feel it's kind of happening in a very kind of smooth way," said Sarfatti. "And probably the earthquake is helping that to happen more just because we do need help, but not necessarily from a colonizing country."

The guardianship the White House has claimed over Venezuela, she said, "is definitely a level of taking over. You can see that when Venezuelan leaders who've been working for 20-something years to recover our country are just set aside."

items: Smith sees no threat to Alberta from U.S.-Venezuela oil deal, renews pipeline push
Federal government will extend gas tax holiday into 2027

blocks.text: The fear now for the Venezuelan opposition is that the Americans' lucrative deal with Rodriguez only gives Washington additional motives to keep her dictatorship in place.
Likewise the U.S. has little motive to demand the release of political prisoners who might challenge the legitimacy of the deal or the government that signed it.
"They were talking about releasing political prisoners, about freedom of press," Sarfatti said. "but then time passed by and Trump's true colours came out.
"We never expected from a country like the U.S., who has been the lead of democracy for so long, to behave the way it's behaving."

articles.title: Alberta separation too costly with too many uncertainties, warns Calgary think-tank
articles.summary: A new report from the Canada West Foundation warns that, though the grievances behind Alberta secession may be real, the economic risks and political uncertainties are too great to consider…

image.caption: A supporter flies an Alberta flag in support of Mitch Sylvestre as he submits his signatures for a separation referendum to Elections Alberta in Edmonton, on May 4, 2026. (Jason Franson/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Calgary

A new report from the Canada West Foundation warns that, though the grievances behind Alberta secession may be real, the economic risks and political uncertainties are too great to consider separating from Canada.
Independent Alberta would cost at least $200B, create ‘murky’ economic future: report
And the Calgary-based public policy think-tank puts a $200 billion price tag on setup costs for an independent Alberta, with a warning at the same time that the province’s economy could shrink.
The report, Alberta in Confederation, breaks down a number of potential separation-related issues, including constitutional negotiations, Indigenous rights, market access and labour supply.
Among the contributors to the report are Ted Morton, former Progressive Conservative MLA and one of the authors of the 2001 firewall letter, and Business Council of Alberta President Adam Legge.

Thursday’s report, which was greeted with criticism from a prominent separatist leader, comes less than two months ahead of the Oct. 19 referendum, where Albertans will vote on whether to remain in Canada, or hold a second, binding referendum on secession.
Canada West Foundation President Gary Mar says the intention is not to settle the debate, but inform voters, and show that the economic future would be “murky.”

"There will be people who will criticize it and say, ‘Look, you're fearmongering.’ This is not fearmongering. This is about laying out the cold hard facts and saying, ‘Here's what you need to know before you cast your vote.'"
Economic consequences
In the report, former Treasury Board senior manager Lennie Kaplan estimates setting up an independent Alberta would cost more than $200 billion, with ongoing costs of more than $50 billion annually.

That would include Alberta taking over its share of the federal net debt, the associated annual debt servicing costs, setting up new trade agreements, and taking over federal transfers for health care, child care and other services.
"Moreover, it could very well shrink Alberta’s economy, cause jobs to be lost, raise interest rates and deter investment," Kaplan writes.

The report warns of the loss of influence over monetary policy decisions if Alberta were to assume the U.S. dollar as its currency, or if a new republic continued using the Canadian dollar despite no longer being in Confederation.

It also calculates that the debt per person in Alberta could rise to between $80,000 and $95,000 post-separation, compared to the $27,000 per person in 2024, based on the increased debt share Alberta might assume if the province left.
The province is putting its own report together costing out potential expenses related to separation. Premier Danielle Smith gave an early estimate of $400 billion earlier this summer.
Impact on workers, students

The Canada West Foundation report questions whether an independent Alberta could attract enough workers to sustain its labour market, particularly if it were to significantly boost its oil production.
Mar noted that much of the province’s current workforce is made up of people from other parts of Canada and the world.
LISTEN | What might Alberta separation mean for workers?:
Radio Active8:59What might Alberta separation mean for workers?
"Is Alberta going to be able to attract such people to come to Alberta when really people who immigrate to Canada come to Canada, they don't come to Alberta," said Mar.
The report also warns of the risk of businesses leaving Alberta, as happened in Quebec around the time of its last sovereignty referendum.
"Most importantly, every Albertan should ask themselves one simple question: Can they be certain their employer, or their job, will still be here if Alberta chooses to separate?" writes Legge.
Post-secondary students could also be affected, the report warns, if they seek schooling in other Canadian provinces and are now subject to international tuition fees.
Constitutional questions
How easy it would actually be for Alberta to secede from Canada has already been the subject of much debate.
The report makes the case that negotiations would be complex, with no guaranteed outcome or agreement from all provinces.
There is also no set timeline, with the potential for "years of negotiation efforts on a wide range of topics," law professor Dwight Newman writes.

Likewise, negotiations with Indigenous people would be “challenging and require significant expert resources to address,” writes political scientist Audrey Doerr, that could require new internal boundaries in the province around First Nations land.
Separatist response

Lawyer Keith Wilson, who co-heads the pro-separation third party advertiser Let Alberta Decide, said in a post on X that the Canada West Foundation report identifies many of the same complications his own team’s analysis has.
But he says the report differs in its assumptions about how those issues would unfold.

"Too often, the Canada West analysis takes an uncertainty or negotiating risk and then assumes a worst-case outcome and ignores Alberta’s powerful leverage. Identifying a risk is not the same as demonstrating that it cannot be planned for, negotiated or managed," Wilson wrote.
Mar says the driving dissatisfactions behind the separatist movement are not to be discounted.
"But we also have to acknowledge that Canada has been good for Alberta in so many ways in terms of the things that we really take for granted," Mar said.
For Wilson, acknowledging Albertans’ grievances does not go far enough.

"The report offers no concrete or enforceable roadmap for ensuring they will actually be fixed. Its answer is essentially to remain in Canada and continue pressing Ottawa for change," Wilson posted on social media.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jennifer is a reporter with CBC Calgary. Previously, she worked for CTV News in Toronto. You can reach her at jennifer.keiller@cbc.ca

articles.title: Transplanted pig kidney works in US man's body for record 271 days
articles.summary: A man has lived for a record nine months with a transplanted pig kidney while waiting for a human transplant.

blocks.text: A kidney transplanted from a pig has worked inside a patient for 271 days – the longest on record, say US doctors.
Tim Andrews said the transplant gave him "hope" and spared him months of needing to go to hospital to have his blood filtered by a dialysis machine.
The team at Mass General Brigham hospital say their work shows pig organs can be used as a "bridge" until a human transplant becomes available.
But the pig organ eventually failed and was removed so Andrews needed a short bout of dialysis before a donor was found.
Doctors and scientists are exploring xenotransplantation – using organs from other species – due to shortages of organs for transplants.
In the US, around 100,000 people are waiting for a kidney while only 25,000 transplants occur each year. More than 7,000 people in the UK are on the kidney transplant list.
Andrews was told it could take seven years to get to the top of the list, but that people live only five years, on average, on dialysis.
"I had a little bit of a shortage of time… it becomes very depressing," he said.
But he described the idea of a pig transplant as "hope" and the "light at the end of the tunnel".
"Hope is the biggest thing, the chance to be free from the [dialysis] machine and live your life."

articles.title: US investigating if missile hit Iran wedding, Vance says
articles.summary: The Iranian Red Crescent Society (IRCS) said shrapnel from a missile hit the ceremony and killed four people on Tuesday.

blocks.text: Watch: JD Vance "extremely sceptical" over alleged strike on Iranian wedding
The US military is investigating Iranian claims that its strikes killed at least four people including two children at a wedding in southern Iran, Vice-President JD Vance has said.

The Iranian Red Crescent Society (IRCS) - a humanitarian group - said shrapnel from a missile hit the ceremony at a home in Sirik on Tuesday, prompting Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei to declare it a "war crime".
US missiles were fired the same day over "attempted attacks" by Iran on American forces, but a US Central Command spokesperson said it "never targets civilians".
Speaking on Thursday, Vance said he was "extremely sceptical" over reports of the alleged strike but confirmed the US would investigate.
"I will say that the Iranian state media has not been a very good scribe about what's happened in the conflict thus far. So I'm extremely sceptical of this," Vance told a White House briefing.
"I know that we're investigating."
Iran has launched fresh attacks on US bases in Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates in response to the alleged strike.

The IRCS said 67 people were hurt when shrapnel from the missile hit a family wedding ceremony, killing at least four people. Iranian state media said a fifth person, a woman aged 22, had died in hospital shortly after.
The four people killed were named locally as Zarkhatoon Taheri, 50; Kolsum Mallahi Nazhdnia, 43; Mohammad Mallahi, 16; and Amirali Karimi, four.

blocks.caption: Image caption, A picture distributed by the Iranian Red Crescent Society purportedly showing the remains of a building which was hosting the wedding ceremony

blocks.text: Image source, Iranian Red Crescent Society
A picture distributed by the Iranian Red Crescent Society purportedly showing the remains of a building which was hosting the wedding ceremony

BBC Verify confirmed a video and two images taken on Tuesday near Kuhestak's coast that showed a telecommunications tower being destroyed, and other videos from Tuesday and Wednesday showed severely damaged houses about 130m (427ft) north of the tower.
BBC Persian Forensics found the telecommunications tower was about 112m (367 ft) from the house where the wedding was being held.
Fighting with Iran has continued for over half a year since the US and Israel launched a joint attack on the country on 28 February.

articles.title: Volkswagen confirms it will cut 100,000 jobs by 2030
articles.summary:
Under-pressure carmaker will shed 15% of workforce and halve its product line in sector’s biggest ever restructure

The car company Volkswagen has confirmed that it will shed 100,000 jobs by…

blocks.text: The car company Volkswagen has announced it will shed 100,000 jobs by the end of the decade after being hit by US tariffs and fierce competition from Chinese rivals.
The German manufacturer said management and unions had agreed as part of a sweeping cost-cutting plan to cut a further 50,000 positions by 2030, bringing total job losses in the pipeline to 100,000.

The number of car models the Volkswagen group produces, which includes the Bentley and Audi brands, will be slashed by half, while four production plants in Germany could also be shuttered within the next eight years.
“It is essential to systematically align workforce levels with economic realities,” Volkswagen group said in a statement.
The company said it had approved a plan that involved “the reduction of about 50,000 jobs”, on top of another 50,000 already agreed.

Volkswagen’s chief executive, Oliver Blume, was booed last month by staff during a tour of the company’s headquarters in Wolfsburg, northern Germany, as part of a company dialogue about the need to address its financial challenges.

At the time, Blume’s restructuring plans, which were rumoured to envisage increasing the reduction in headcount from 50,000 to 100,000, were yet to be approved by the VW group’s powerful supervisory board, which represents the labour force and shareholders.
But on Thursday, the company, Europe’s largest carmaker, said the board had signed-off on the proposals.
“The supervisory board has unanimously approved the executive board’s future plan presented today,” Blume said. “This is a strong signal for the future of the Volkswagen group.”
The total of 100,000 cuts will be the largest restructuring ever carried out in the global automotive industry, amounting to about 15% of the carmaker’s employees.
Volkswagen employs more than 650,000 people across all its brands, which also includes Skoda, Seat, Porsche, Cupra and Lamborghini.
On Thursday, Volkswagen also said that management and unions agreed that the future of four German plants – in Hanover, Emden, Zwickau and Neckarsulm – could not be guaranteed into the 2030s.

VW has faced increasing pressure from rampant Chinese competition in Europe, decreasing sales in China and hefty US tariffs. Even before that, it was struggling for years with falling profits and overproduction in Europe.

The tough market in China has also hit other carmakers, with BMW cutting its profit guidance for this year because of the disruption caused by the Iran war and the company’s struggles in the Chinese market.

articles.title: DMW: 2 Filipinos dead in Strait of Hormuz attack
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Migrant Workers (DMW) has reported the death of two Filipino seafarers on board the Saudi-flagged crude oil tanker SIDR which was hit by unidentified…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Migrant Workers (DMW) has reported the death of two Filipino seafarers on board the Saudi-flagged crude oil tanker SIDR which was hit by unidentified projectiles as it was about to cross the Strait of Hormuz.

Migrant Workers Secretary Hans Cacdac said in a press briefing on Wednesday that the victims were among 16 Filipino seafarers on the vessel when it was attacked on Aug. 31. The rest were unharmed with the vessel now off the coast of Oman.
“Unfortunately, we have two crew members who died as a result of the attack,” Cacdac told reporters, adding that a fire broke out on the tanker but it was contained by the crew.
“We are already working on the immediate repatriation of all the crew members, including the two fatalities,” he said.
According to the DMW chief, he would personally visit the families of the victims although he did not disclose where they reside, citing privacy concerns.

The DMW and the Overseas Workers Welfare Administration will also provide assistance to the families while government agencies coordinate with authorities in Oman on the repatriation of the Filipino seafarers, Cacdac said.
President Marcos has likewise ordered that assistance be given to the victims’ families, Palace Press Officer Claire Castro said on Thursday.

“First and foremost, the President and the administration extend their condolences to the families of the two seafarers from Cabuyao, Laguna, and Daanbantayan, Cebu. The President has also ordered immediate assistance for the families of our two fellow citizens who perished, as well as the provision of all necessary support—including the benefits, compensation and insurance proceeds—rightfully due to them,” Castro said in a briefing at the Malancañang.
“The government will not neglect the families left behind by our two fellow citizens. Once again, we extend our condolences to the families of our two seafarers,” she added.

The DMW, meanwhile, remains on red alert amid continuing security risks in the Strait of Hormuz, Cacdac said. According to him, they were coordinating with the Department of National Defense and the Department of Foreign Affairs on the security situation involving Filipino seafarers in the region.
About 3,000 Filipino seafarers remain aboard vessels in the wider Persian Gulf, although they are not necessarily all within the Strait of Hormuz, Cacdac said.
High-risk area
