Since Feb. 28, when the United States and Israel launched an attack on Iran, triggering the Middle East conflict, about 31 ships carrying 421 Filipino seafarers have been attacked while entering or leaving the strait.
Cacdac said that 268 of those seafarers have since returned to the Philippines. Of the 421, 406 were unharmed, 10 were injured but had recovered, three had died and one remains officially missing.

The DMW, however, is not imposing a blanket deployment ban on Filipino seafarers passing through the Strait of Hormuz unlike its policy covering the Northern Black Sea, because of the strategic importance of the waterway and the principle of freedom of navigation, he added.

Instead, shipowners must conduct risk assessments before voyages and ensure that adequate security measures are in place, including security protocols, possible escorts, armed guards and reporting mechanisms, he said.
“We are disallowing deployment to the extent that there is a refusal of sailing by the seafarer,” Cacdac stressed.
He said that the right of Filipino seafarers to refuse sailing in high-risk areas must be respected.
The DMW will investigate the incident, including whether the appropriate safety and risk-assessment measures were followed.

Cacdac said the SIDR appeared to have been heading toward the Strait of Hormuz after coming from the eastern coast of the United Arab Emirates and sailing northward off Oman, but the vessel’s exact route remains subject to further determination.
For now, it is still too early to provide details on how the two Filipino seafarers died, he noted.
“It is not yet clear how exactly that happened. Usually, when we are still 24 to 48 hours removed from the event, we will find out the details as we go along,” Cacdac said.

He added that the DMW remains in contact with Bahri, the Saudi shipping company in charge of the vessel, and would meet with its top management to discuss the incident and the safety of Filipino crew members. /das

articles.title: Iran war is not a war, US VP Vance says
articles.summary: WASHINGTON, United States — U.S. Vice President JD Vance said Thursday he would not categorize the Iran war as a war, despite continuing clashes with Tehran six months after the start of the…

blocks.text: WASHINGTON, United States — U.S. Vice President JD Vance said Thursday he would not categorize the Iran war as a war, despite continuing clashes with Tehran six months after the start of the conflict.
Vance’s comments came amid growing signs that President Donald Trump is trying to draw a line under the conflict that has bogged down his administration.
“I wouldn’t call it a war. Right now, there is no active shooting,” Vance told a White House briefing when asked if the war would be over by the U.S. midterm elections in November.
Vance added that “I recognize there have been places where this has flared up,” but said major combat operations only lasted for six weeks after the U.S.-Israel war started on Feb. 28.

“But when you ask when will this end, you’re asking me a question like when will the Iranians stop shooting at ships? I think the reality is I don’t know the answer to that question. You would have to ask the Iranians,” he said.
After several weeks of calm, fresh clashes began with U.S. raids on Sunday, deepening the impasse in the six-month war, as Iran maintains a stranglehold on the strategic Strait of Hormuz.
Vance insisted that the United States would not reopen talks with Iran until it ended attacks on commercial shipping.

But with fuel prices threatening to cost Trump’s Republicans their control of Congress at the ballot box, his administration has begun pushing the message that oil flows through the waterway are now returning to pre-war levels.
Wedding strike probe
“Their control over the Strait of Hormuz is effectively gone,” Vance said of Iran.

“If you go back three months ago, how much oil and gas was coming out of the strait under Iranian threats? It was virtually nothing. Now, it’s almost back to where it was before the conflict even started,” Vance said.
Trump’s approval ratings are near record lows as the president who vowed to keep the United States out of any more foreign wars finds himself in a quagmire with the Islamic Republic.
Eighteen U.S. troops and thousands of people in Iran and Lebanon have died in the conflict since February.
The Wall Street Journal reported that Trump was now discussing with senior aides whether to declare the Iran war over. He posted a photo of a banner saying “Mission Accomplished” last week.
Iran pressed on with fresh attacks on Thursday, saying it hit U.S. military bases in Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates to avenge a strike on a wedding that it blamed on Washington.
Vance said the United States was probing the wedding strike but cast doubt on Iranian reporting of the incident.

“I know that we’re investigating,” Vance said. “I will say that the Iranian state media has not been a very good source of information about what’s happened in the conflict thus far. So I’m extremely skeptical of this.”
The Iranian Red Crescent said the missile attack on the wedding in the Iranian coastal town of Kuhestak killed four people late Tuesday, including a child, and wounded more than 50. /das

articles.title: ‘Friend-for-hire’ services gain traction in Thailand
articles.summary: “Friend-for-hire” services have started taking off in Thailand as the country’s social landscape changes with an aging population and a rise in the number of unmarried people. The service is a new…

blocks.text: “Friend-for-hire” services have started taking off in Thailand as the country’s social landscape changes with an aging population and a rise in the number of unmarried people.
The service is a new type of gig work in which people are paid to act as companions, for instance accompanying someone on a trip to take photos or even joining them in indoor rock climbing.

Although no official figures are available, industry players say demand for professional companions has increased in recent years due to the rise in people living alone, changing lifestyles and the influence of social media.
According to global market research company Euromonitor International, 29.5 percent of Thai households were single-person households in 2025, exceeding the global average of 21.9 percent.
And that growing segment has created rising demand for products and services designed for independent living, such as single-seat restaurant tables and solo travel.
For many clients, however, the motivation for hiring a companion is convenience rather than loneliness.

Ainthuon Rattanawaraporn, a university student and content creator from Bangkok, said she initially used the service out of curiosity but soon found it solved a problem—friends were sometimes too busy to come with her on trips but she was not yet comfortable traveling alone.
“I also wanted someone to take pictures for me,” she said.
Unlike asking friends for favors, hiring a companion allowed her to freely request specific photo angles and compositions because photography was part of the service.
“I don’t want to bother my friends by asking them to take hundreds of photos during a trip,” she said. “With a hired companion, I can tell them exactly what kind of pictures I want.”
Growing demand
The growing demand has created new income opportunities for people like Thanaporn Charoenchuea, a 20-year-old university student who started her “Snap Like a Bestie” service.
Within about two months, she had served more than 50 clients. She said her customers are not simply looking for someone to take photographs.
“They want someone who can make them feel comfortable while capturing natural-looking photos,” she said.
Apart from taking photos, Thanaporn spends much of her time chatting with clients, helping shy or introverted people relax before posing for pictures.

“The biggest challenge is making sure every client enjoys both the experience and the final photos,” she said. “I love photography and meeting new people, so I find the job both enjoyable and rewarding.”
On busy days, she accepts up to three appointments, each lasting between one and three hours. She only accepts bookings in public places after screening clients through their social media accounts.
For another companion service provider, Penkawin Wangniwetkul, known as Ice, the business has evolved well beyond photography.

After leaving her full-time job as a television coproducer, Ice spent several years working as a presenter, master of ceremonies, and online marketing host before entering the companionship business about three months ago.
The opportunity came unexpectedly after relatives suggested she accompany two elderly women on shopping trips and outings.
“I realized there was genuine demand for someone who could simply accompany people,” she said, adding that she later began posting about the experience on social media, leading to more referrals.

Today, clients hire her for activities, including running, gym workouts, aerobics, shopping, spa visits, cafe hopping, and even indoor rock climbing. A typical booking lasts two to three hours, and she charges 1,000 baht ($30) per hour.
Ice has served more than 10 clients and intentionally limits bookings because she continues to work as an MC and presenter. She also screens every client before accepting an assignment.

Her clients have included public figures, including an actress she accompanied to a veterinary clinic. She has also received requests to attend wedding receptions as a companion, although she was too busy to accept.

Despite growing demand, Ice is selective. She turns down requests that could compromise her safety or make her feel uncomfortable, including accompanying male clients to late-night entertainment venues.
Outside city trips
The service has also expanded to trips outside the city. Company employee Sasiprapa Nookong is among those who hired a companion during a trip to Chiang Mai.

Sasiprapa said that while traveling with a friend, they decided to spend one day pursuing different interests. Her friend planned to go hiking, while she preferred visiting cafes around the city, so she contacted a university student offering the service after seeing reviews on TikTok.

“I believe this service meets the needs of people who occasionally want company, not long-term companionship,” she said, echoing others in stressing that safety should always come first when hiring strangers.

Sociologist Narupon Duangwises of the Princess Maha Chakri Sirindhorn Anthropology Centre wrote in a report that interacting with hired companions may provide emotional comfort for people who find it difficult to make friends in everyday life.

But he noted that one feature distinguishing “friends for hire” from traditional friendship is the ability to choose a companion based on physical appearance, unlike friendships that develop naturally.
He therefore suggested that service providers establish clear rules and boundaries to protect themselves and prevent situations, such as sexual harassment or other forms of violence. /das

articles.title: El Niño could be strongest in decades, UN warns
articles.summary: GENEVA, Switzerland — El Niño is forecast to be the strongest since comparable records began four decades ago, the United Nations’ climate agency warned Thursday, with the UN chief saying the world…

blocks.text: GENEVA, Switzerland — El Niño is forecast to be the strongest since comparable records began four decades ago, the United Nations’ climate agency warned Thursday, with the UN chief saying the world was in the “danger zone of extreme weather.”
The weather phenomenon is set to become “very strong” in the months ahead and is almost certain to persist through February, the World Meteorological Organization said.
“If this trajectory continues, it may be stronger than anything since our monitoring began,” WMO chief Celeste Saulo told reporters in Geneva.
El Niño will peak toward the end of this year — though its knock-on effects on the climate will continue well into 2027, said the WMO.
El Niño warms surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, bringing worldwide changes in winds, pressure and rainfall.
Heat in the oceans is released more slowly into the atmosphere, pushing up global temperatures the year after it develops.
The powerful 2023-24 El Niño contributed to 2024 being the warmest year on record, and “we should not be surprised if this record is broken,” Saulo added.

“El Niño is firmly established and will intensify into a very strong event in the coming months, with big impacts on rainfall and temperature patterns and associated risks of floods, drought and extreme heat,” the WMO said.
Highway to the danger zone
El Niño is a naturally occurring phenomenon and is not caused by climate change.
But scientists expect it will exacerbate the heat of a planet already warming from burning fossil fuels, while amplifying weather extremes.
“El Niño is being supersized before our eyes,” said UN chief Antonio Guterres.

“The science leaves no room for doubt: The planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up. Sea surface temperatures are rising, temperatures keep climbing, and the world is in the danger zone of extreme weather.”
WMO chief Saulo urged disaster management authorities and climate-sensitive sectors like agriculture, fisheries, health, energy and water to prepare themselves.
“This exceptional El Niño … has the potential to deliver a massive blow to communities and economies across the world,” she said.
“We are already seeing disruption and devastation from droughts and floods, and we expect these impacts to increase as El Niño intensifies.”
El Niño typically takes place every two to seven years and lasts around nine to 12 months.
Conditions oscillate between El Niño and its opposite, La Niña, with neutral conditions in between.
El Niño can reshape weather and climate patterns thousands of kilometers away from the tropical Pacific.
Pacific Ocean heating up

Wilfran Moufouma-Okia, the WMO’s climate prediction chief, said some places would be affected before, some during and some after the peak later this year — though the strength of the peak is not an indicator of the severity of the impact.
For September-November, WMO forecasts indicate an increased likelihood of above-normal temperatures “across almost all land areas.”
The index, which measures sea surface temperature anomalies in the central eastern equatorial Pacific, has strengthened from an average 1.5°C above normal between May and July.
Weekly values between late July and mid-August ranged from around 2.2°C to 2.6°C above average, indicating continued El Niño intensification.
The UN agency classifies El Niño events as weak, moderate, strong or very strong — meaning this one is set to reach the highest level out of four.
Moufouma-Okia said the classification meant a sea surface temperature anomaly of more than 2°C.
“That category is open: We know where it starts; we don’t know where it ends,” he told AFP.
The average forecast is pointing toward an anomaly peaking at 3.6°C — way higher than the last two very strong El Niños in 1997-98 and 2015-16.
In some areas, subsurface ocean temperatures were more than 8°C above average during July and early August.
Saulo called this a huge reservoir of “very warm ocean waters that will fuel the intensity of El Niño.”
The UN’s International Organization for Migration agency appealed Thursday for $110 million to protect 4.9 million people from the potentially severe impacts of the phenomenon. /das

articles.title: Spacecraft bound for Mercury begins ‘tricky’ arrival
articles.summary: PARIS, France — After an eight-year journey, a spacecraft carrying European and Japanese probes began the months-long, high-risk approach to Mercury on Thursday to study the Sun-scorched planet. The…

blocks.text: PARIS, France — After an eight-year journey, a spacecraft carrying European and Japanese probes began the months-long, high-risk approach to Mercury on Thursday to study the Sun-scorched planet.
The BepiColombo mission set off from Earth in 2018 on a winding path to study the smallest and least understood planet in our solar system, with the aim of releasing the two probes into its orbit.
On Thursday, it began its arrival phase, described by the European Space Agency (ESA) as its “most operationally challenging planetary arrival sequence ever attempted.”

Mercury’s relatively tiny mass — it is only slightly bigger than the moon — means its gravitational pull is extremely weak compared with the Sun’s, making it complicated for spacecraft to approach the planet without ending up incinerated or lost in space.
“It’s a very ambitious mission,” Santa Martinez, the mission manager at ESA, told a press conference ahead of its arrival.
The spacecraft had to travel more than 10 billion kilometers (miles), executing a series of nine flybys, to speed up, slow down and perfect its trajectory.
The two probes, which are attached to each other, finally separated on Thursday from the transfer module that has propelled them — a crucial first step in the final approach.

It was the equivalent of “launching a new spacecraft. Only this spacecraft happens to be around a different planet,” explained Ignacio Tanco, ESA’s head of inner solar system mission operations, before the separation began.
All went to plan
On Thursday, Mercury was some 63 million km from the Sun and 200 million km from Earth.

“At these distances … any real-time operation becomes impossible,” Tanco said, explaining there was about a 30-minute delay between checks being performed and commands being executed from the ground to the spacecraft.
It meant the spacecraft had to check and execute the separation autonomously — a “tricky business,” Tanco said.
But all went to plan.
The spacecraft autonomously cut the four mechanical struts connecting the orbiters to the module.
Spring mechanisms then gently pushed them away.
The separation took place at a speed of 40 centimeters (16 inches) per second, leaving the two entities relatively close given the vastness of space.

Due to the distance between the probes and Earth, the signal confirming the operation’s success reached the control center in Darmstadt, Germany, nearly two hours later — at 1353 GMT — sparking rounds of applause and cheers.
“This is the best-case scenario, that the telemetry comes exactly at the moment we expect it,” said Elsa Montagnon, in charge of module operations at ESA.
“The spacecraft has completed its reconfiguration as expected,” she said with relief.
The probes are due to enter Mercury’s orbit on Nov. 21.
The next tricky phase will come on Dec. 9 and 10, when the two probes separate into their respective orbits.
From April, the ESA’s Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) will begin studying the planet closest to the Sun with unprecedented precision, passing just 480 km from its surface.
The Japanese Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (Mio) will focus on its space environment and magnetic field, following an elliptical orbit that will carry it as far as 11,000 km away.
New chapter
Mercury is the least studied of the four rocky, innermost planets in our solar system, which include Venus, Earth and Mars.
NASA’s Mariner 10 was the first probe to capture a close image of its lunar-looking surface in 1974.
The MESSENGER probe then orbited the planet in 2011.
But many mysteries remain about its magnetic field, iron core and surface marked by hollows.

With its 16 instruments and 1.7-billion-euro ($2.0-billion) budget, BepiColombo “is going to bring to humanity and to the scientific community unprecedented views of Mercury … and it’s going to open a new chapter in our understanding of the solar system,” Martinez said. /das

articles.title: Berlin: BER Airport Terminal 1 reopened after security scare
articles.summary: Police have given the all-clear at Terminal 1 at Berlin's BER Airport following an earlier security scare and evacuation. The airport said some flights had been delayed but they were trying to avoid…

image.caption: Crowds waited outside the terminal building amid the police operationImage: Ann-Marie Utz/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Terminal 1 at Berlin Brandenburg Airport (BER) was reopened on Thursday evening following an earlier evacuation due to a security scare.
"The police operation has ended," said an airport spokeswoman.

Federal police, responsible for transportation security in Germany, had evacuated BER Terminal 1 at around 5:45 p.m. after a woman reportedly told security staff at a service point that she had a dangerous substance in her luggage.
"A potential threat from the unidentified substance could not be ruled out," the police spokesperson told the dpa news agency.
Police then gave the all-clear at around 8:45 p.m. and confirmed that nobody had been in danger at any point.
Police initially provided no information as to the nature of the substance in question, with analysis results expected in the coming days.
Berlin: BER operations remain restricted
Despite the all-clear, operations at BER remained restricted on Thursday evening.
"Due to the police operation, we will still be experiencing delays and some cancelations until the end of the day," said the airport spokeswoman.
She advised travelers to double-check the status of their flight before arriving at BER and to keep an eye on the boards while at the airport.
"Flights were not stopped," she insisted, emphasizing that there were only delays.
"Regular operations will resume on Friday."

blocks.caption: Various emergency services were in action at the scene as dusk fell on ThursdayImage: Michael Ukas/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: What did the airport say about departures and arrivals?
The airport had confirmed the incident itself earlier on Thursday but said planes that were already prepared to depart could take off as normal and incoming arrivals could also continue to land.
Passenger processing was "relocated to Terminal 2 to the extent that it's possible," a spokesperson said.
Many but not all flights departing Terminal 1 from around 7 p.m. local time were marked as delayed on the airport's website.
An airport press officer told DW that around 30 flights had been delayed but that they were trying to avoid cancellations by redirecting departures to Terminal 2.

blocks.caption: Specialist personnel could be seen in action near the buildingImage: Michael Ukas/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Trains were also impacted by the operation for a time. The city's S-Bahn train service confirmed disruptions on both lines to airport, while Deutsche Bahn also reported widespread disruptions to regional trains.

BER or the "Willy Brandt Airport" in Schönefeld is Berlin's busiest and Germany's third-busiest airport since it opened in 2020. It also serves as the primary airport for many federal government flights. Some 26 million passengers travel through it each year.

The last comparable security disruption at the airport was in March of this year, when flights were disrupted but because of a potentially suspicious aerial object rather than a suspicious item in the terminal.

blocks.caption: Personnel responding to the alert went through decontamination procedures on leaving the buildingImage: Michael Ukas/dpa/picture alliance

articles.title: Sleeping Trans-Canada Tesla drivers caught on video in B.C., fined $368
articles.summary: The B.C. Highway Patrol says an officer captured video of a man with his eyes closed and hands off the wheel as his Tesla travelled on through Langley.

image.caption: The BCHP says an officer passed a sleeping driver in a dark-coloured Tesla on Aug. 27 as it sped down the Trans-Canada Highway through Langley. (RCMP)

blocks.text: British Columbia·New
The B.C. Highway Patrol says an officer captured video of a man with his eyes closed and hands off the wheel as his Tesla travelled on through Langley.
The use of full self-driving technology remains illegal in B.C.

The B.C. Highway Patrol (BCHP) is drawing attention to the hazards of people asleep at the wheel after two snoozing drivers in self-driving Teslas were caught on video as they travelled along the Trans-Canada Highway in the Lower Mainland.
"Police will not debate the merits of self-driving technology with sleeping drivers. It's illegal in B.C., and we're here to enforce the law and keep roads safe," said BCHP Sgt. Michael McLaughlin.
The BCHP says an officer passed a sleeping driver in a dark-coloured Tesla on Aug. 27 as it sped down the Trans-Canada Highway through Langley.
McLaughlin said the officer had to prioritize the Tesla driver over the call he was supposed to attend after observing the man had his eyes closed and wasn't holding the steering wheel.

Nap on your couch? Sounds like a plan.
Sleep in your car? That’s a $368 dollar ticket.
A Langley driver is the latest person in BC to put others at risk by sleeping in heavy traffic.https://t.co/1Ob6KvJtlf pic.twitter.com/UUE51Ek6pA—BCHwyPatrol
The man was fined $368 for driving without due care and attention and $81 for failing to produce a driver's licence.

items: Where B.C. stands on self-driving cars and what recent incidents reveal about safety, rules
B.C. bans self-driving vehicles on its roads

blocks.text: "The potential for serious injury or death is too high. If you're sleeping, you're forcing us to pull you over, and that means we're going to leave you with financial consequences," McLaughlin said.
Police say a different Tesla driver was handed a similar $368 fine after she was caught on video asleep at the wheel on the Trans-Canada in North Vancouver on Aug. 11.

We’re not here to debate the technology.
On August 11, Highway #1 in North Vancouver, this woman was ticketed $368. Two witnesses agreed to testify in court.
The law requires that you are fully alert and focused on driving.https://t.co/uCSTBjOmeG pic.twitter.com/eLa2gb04My—BCHwyPatrol
The video was taken by a passenger in another car and shared with police.
The B.C. Highway Patrol said it was able to identify the driver as a Maple Ridge resident and registered owner of the Tesla.

items: Viral video appears to show woman asleep behind the wheel on busy B.C. highway

blocks.text: In July, video appearing to show a sleeping Tesla driver on the busy Trans-Canada Highway near Revelstoke went viral.
Fred Lambert, editor-in-chief at Electrek.co, said Tesla's driver monitoring system, which is supposed to ensure a driver doesn't fall asleep, can easily be bypassed.
Lambert says as self-driving technology evolves, some drivers are becoming complacent.
"We're entering a weird time right now when it comes to these advanced driver-assist systems," he said.

"I've seen videos of people posting video of themselves playing video games in the driver's seat, I've seen people watching movies. People don't realize this is extremely dangerous and also purely illegal."
B.C.'s Motor Vehicle Act prohibits the use of highly automated self-driving vehicles on public roads, although lesser automated features like lane change assist or automatic braking are allowed.
The Ministry of Transportation website says highly automated self-driving vehicles are a new and emerging technology that require further testing and policy development.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Karin Larsen is a former Olympian and award-winning sports broadcaster who covers news and sports for CBC Vancouver.
With files from Caroline Barghout

articles.title: Accountability, not resilience
articles.summary: If there’s any consolation in these gray overcast days, it’s that the word “resilience” has lost its shine, and is now regarded as a curse dooming us to a relentless cycle of calamities, the most…

blocks.text: If there’s any consolation in these gray overcast days, it’s that the word “resilience” has lost its shine, and is now regarded as a curse dooming us to a relentless cycle of calamities, the most recent being the record-high floods that have sunk lives, homes, and livelihood.
Indeed, this misplaced pride over the Filipinos’ capacity to survive insurmountable odds has given government officials a free pass from accountability for failing to do their job.

According to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council, the combined effects of the southwest monsoon and last month’s tropical cyclones have affected at least 8.8 million individuals or 2.5 million families, and left 39 dead, 18 injured, and three missing across regions. Tens of thousands remain in evacuation centers while many more were stranded in areas suddenly cut off by rampaging floods and cascading mudslides.

Meanwhile, motorists on North Luzon Expressway (NLEx) found themselves stuck in traffic for as long as 22 hours with vehicle buildup of up to 10 kilometers (km), as the San Simon, Pampanga portion of the toll road was inundated by floods too hazardous to cross. A similar situation in 2023 led NLEx management to raise the level of affected roads, which apparently did not help much.
Human cost

The human cost of the disastrous floods is all too tragic in the case of 25-year-old Reiner Novero, who was caught on CCTV walking along a flooded sidewalk in Barangay Cutcut, Angeles City when he suddenly disappeared. An open drainage canal completely hidden by floodwaters had swallowed him, with his body later recovered 2 km downstream. Then there is the case of four passengers of a sport utility vehicle that fell into the Tarlac River after the Agana Bridge partially collapsed, with two bodies recovered so far.

The callous disregard for the welfare of constituents was underscored by this mayor who brazenly told them to fend for themselves and “build a second floor” to their homes to escape the floods, basically to adjust to the harsh reality.

Faced with such cavalier attitude, surely it’s time to exact accountability from officials elected to serve the public? While investigation into failed flood control projects has led to several lawmakers and contractors charged with graft and plunder, little seems to be done to ensure the continued viability and safety of existing public works and infrastructures. Should officials just wait until they buckle down, like the Agana and the Aquino bridges in Tarlac?
Criminal neglect

The collapse of retaining walls and roads that clearly show the lack of steel girders and standard supports should be raised as criminal neglect against the contractors and project proponents of these substandard structures. Government too must start identifying sites for water retention facilities to prevent the overflow of swollen creeks and rivers

As well, NLEx management should take full responsibility for the hours-long gridlock on the expressway owing to the San Simon floods, considering it had happened before and should have led it to explore more lasting engineering solutions to the perennial flooding.

As irate motorists have pointed out, they pay tolls to ensure a faster trip, proper road maintenance, traffic management, and in times of emergency that necessitate rerouting, proper coordination with local authorities to facilitate matters. In this case, motorists diverted from the flooded expressway found themselves on risky tertiary roads that traversed rice fields and irrigation canals, and some that led to dead-ends.
More logical response

Admittedly, climate change has a lot to do with the spate of storms that dumped more rains than usual in parts of the country, but aggravating factors for the deluge can be traced to human greed and neglect: denuded forests from mining and commercial development, failed flood control projects, waterways silted with garbage and plastic waste.

Instead of turning to Filipino resilience for customary comfort, it may be time to convert that into collective defiance as Cardinal Pablo David has urged in his Facebook post. Time to ask the crucial questions: where did the billions in public works budget go? Who designed and built the structures? What maintenance steps were taken to keep them safe and serviceable? Which politician sponsored what project—and probably pocketed millions from them?

But accountability cuts both ways and citizens must be held responsible as well. Proper garbage disposal, documenting leaks, cracks, and apparent weaknesses in public works and calling government attention to them, and starting a community reforestation campaign are some initiatives that can help.

Still, there’s a simpler, more logical response to these chronic calamities brought on by government incompetence: voting for candidates based on their record of public service. It’s time to replace resilience with long memories over unkept promises and willful neglect.

articles.title: Trees, water in the Season of Creation
articles.summary: Last Tuesday, Sept. 1, Pope Leo XIV launched the World Day of Prayer for the Care of Creation, which marked the beginning of the Season of Creation (that ends on Oct. 4, Feast of St. Francis of…

blocks.text: Last Tuesday, Sept. 1, Pope Leo XIV launched the World Day of Prayer for the Care of Creation, which marked the beginning of the Season of Creation (that ends on Oct. 4, Feast of St. Francis of Assisi) observed by people from various Christian denominations all over the world, and with the theme “living water.” Caring for our common home, the Pope said, calls for a conversion of heart so that what had been used to bring about destruction may instead be directed toward life. “I invite everyone to join in prayer and action that we may become channels of the living water of God’s peace, refreshing our wounded world.”

The Pope also invited the faithful and all people of goodwill to safeguard water, to consider it with gratitude, justice, and responsibility and as “a right without borders.” He said: “Imagine a hot summer day after hard work or a long walk and you finally take a sip of cold water. You have relief and energy flow through your body. Moments like these remind us what a blessing clean water is. Yet one in four people worldwide still lack safe drinking water. Entire communities and nations need our action and our prayer for the care of water, for the blessed relief…”

One cannot mistake his equating water with life and the quenching of thirst whether literally or figuratively. I was watching and reflecting on all that while hereabouts, millions of Filipinos were submerged not in “living water” but in killer waters that swept through major parts of Central Luzon, the National Capital Region, and several provinces during the latter part of August and in early September. And think about the “tsunami from the mountains” that cascaded on Nepal when a killer glacier detached itself from the Himalayan mountains and carried with it such unprecedented destructive force that buried structures, people, and other living things in the plains.

Right smack into the launch of the Season of Creation was the call of Bishop Broderick Pabillo of the vicariate of Taytay in Palawan for a stop to the killing of primeval forests to give way to mining operations. Palawan is considered the Philippines’ “last frontier” because many areas still remain as they are since the beginning of time, so to speak. I have been in various areas in Palawan many times, and while each area is unique, the virgin forests are the single mainstay to behold that must be guarded. Not being a natural scientist, I have always wondered about the wondrous life forms and beings that thrive therein, the vulnerable, the yet undiscovered.

At the opening Mass this week of the national convention of the Conference of Major Superiors in the Philippines held in Zamboanga City, Bishop Pabillo raised the alarm on what might be the felling of 57,000 trees in Southern Palawan to give way to a mining project. “You can plant trees, but you cannot replant the forest,” Bishop Pabillo said, questioning the term “reforestation” as a replacement for the forests destroyed. The bishop is also chair of the Catholic Bishops’ Conference of the Philippines’ Office on Stewardship. He called the use of the word reforestation “a lie.”

According to Palawan Daily, the 57,000 trees that Bishop Pabillo mentioned are different from the figure used by another Palawan bishop, Socrates Mesiona, who questioned the government’s Special Tree Cutting and Earth Balling Permits to cover at least 218,854 trees in Palawan areas. I thought, how do you ball a forest tree and use it for “reforestation” somewhere else?
In my mind is the popular saying, “A tree grows, a tree dies, the forest lives forever.”
Beloved poet, philosopher, and environmentalist Wendell Berry passed away recently at age 92. Here are excerpts from his poem “I go among the trees”:
I go among the trees and sit still/ All my stirring becomes quiet/ like circles on water,/ My tasks lie in their places/ where I left them, asleep like cattle.
Then what is afraid of me comes/ and lives a while in my sight./ What it fears in me leaves me/ and the fear of me leaves it./ It sings and I hear its song…
After days of labor,/ mute in my consternations,/ I hear my song at last,/ and I sing it. As we sing,/ the day turns, the trees move.
Send feedback to cerespd@gmail.com

articles.title: The fury of the Nepal fall
articles.summary: Tremor. Avalanche. Internal tsunami. The catastrophic flash floods that tore through the Nepal-Tibet border along the Trishuli and Bhote Koshi river systems serve as a grim masterclass in modern…

blocks.text: Tremor. Avalanche. Internal tsunami. The catastrophic flash floods that tore through the Nepal-Tibet border along the Trishuli and Bhote Koshi river systems serve as a grim masterclass in modern disaster science. Historically, conventional disaster management models treated earthquakes, landslides, avalanches, and floods as isolated, linear phenomena. However, the August 2026 Himalayan deluge underscores a more complex geological reality—the concept of “cascading hazards.” In high-altitude, seismically active mountain ranges, these disasters do not merely occur sequentially. They are fundamentally entangled, with one event serving as the energetic trigger, amplifier, or chemical accelerator for the next.

The recent disaster initially presented a scientific paradox. Early geophysical data captured a sudden seismic signal equivalent to a magnitude 4.4 to 5.2 earthquake near Langtang Lirung. This led authorities to assume a tectonic earthquake had shaken loose the mountain’s crust. However, subsequent wave analysis by the United States Geological Survey revealed a shocking inverse reality: there was no prerequisite tectonic earthquake. Instead, the massive kinetic energy generated by an enormous mass of rock and ice collapsing down the mountainside was so violent that it registered as an earthquake on global seismometers. This phenomenon demonstrates how the boundaries between landslides and earthquakes blur in extreme topographies. A massive mass movement behaves like a localized seismic hammer. When millions of tons of alpine material drop thousands of feet, the energy transfer into the Earth’s crust generates long-period seismic waves. This seismic energy radiates outward, potentially destabilizing adjacent, highly fractured slopes. What begins as a localized failure can rapidly transform into a self-perpetuating regional shake, triggering secondary structural failures across a highly sensitive mountain ecosystem.

The core engine of this 2026 flood was not heavy monsoon rainfall, but a violent, hybrid rock-ice avalanche. According to observations from the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development, a massive section of a glacier—roughly 2,000 feet wide—sheared from an altitude of over 5,000 meters. As this colossal sheet of ice collapsed, it merged with a massive rock landslide. The science behind this entanglement relies on thermal and frictional dynamics. As the rock and ice mixture tumbled down vertical valley walls at speeds exceeding 120 miles per hour, intense friction generated extreme thermal energy. This pulverized and flash-melted portions of the glacial ice instantly. Simultaneously, the charging avalanche acted as a monstrous plow, scouring the valley floor to scrape up waterlogged monsoon sediment, gravel, and massive boulders. The transition from a frozen, solid alpine slope to a liquid, hypermobile debris flow represents a profound state change. Solid ice becomes the very lubricant that drives the solid rock landslide forward, creating a highly destructive slurry far more dense and lethal than typical water floods.

The final link in this cascading chain occurred when this hypervelocity debris slammed into the Lhende Khola river valley. When an avalanche of this scale impacts a narrow mountain river corridor, it acts as an instantaneous, natural earth dam. The river is abruptly choked off, forcing water to back up rapidly into an artificial lake. Because these landslide dams are composed of loose, unconsolidated sediment, ice, and rock, they possess no structural integrity. As the water pressure behind the blockage builds to a critical tipping point, the dam suffers a catastrophic, instantaneous breach. The result is an “inland tsunami”—a wall of pulverized ice, thick mud, and rocks that surged down the Trishuli River corridor, rising up to 9 meters in just 30 minutes. The fluid dynamics involved in such a debris surge is devastating. The immense weight of the sediment increases the flow’s momentum, enabling it to easily snap concrete bridges, crush hydropower dams, and erase entire villages from the map.

Hovering precariously over this interconnected science is the undeniable footprint of climate change. This sustained warming directly destabilizes the mountain cryosphere. As atmospheric temperatures rise, meltwater seeps deep into alpine rock fractures. When this water undergoes freeze-thaw cycles, it expands, fracturing bedrock via frost wedging. Furthermore, the degradation of high-altitude permafrost (the ancient frozen soil acting as the structural “glue” of the mountains) weakens the structural integrity of mountain peaks.

An avalanche is no longer just falling snow, a landslide is no longer just a collapsing hill, and an earthquake is no longer just moving faults. In the Anthropocene, they are deeply entangled components of a volatile, cascading geological engine. Deciphering the physics of these compounded interactions is no longer just an academic pursuit. It is a vital prerequisite for building early-warning systems capable of protecting vulnerable downstream communities.
Dr. Joel Tiu Maquiling may be reached at jmaquiling@ateneo.edu

articles.title: Stories of history
articles.summary: There was a time when the various national shrines dedicated to our heroes were run by family members or descendants of the heroes commemorated. When I first visited the Emilio Aguinaldo Shrine in…

blocks.text: There was a time when the various national shrines dedicated to our heroes were run by family members or descendants of the heroes commemorated. When I first visited the Emilio Aguinaldo Shrine in Kawit in the 1980s, my classmate and I were met by Linda Aguinaldo. We drove from Manila to Cavite in less than an hour. Being a weekday, there were no other visitors, so Linda not only showed us the Aguinaldo mansion, but also narrated how they played around the mansion and explored its many secret passages. She brought us up the watch tower (mirador) from where, on a clear day, Aguinaldo could see Manila. She showed the veranda, near the kitchen, where the general had his regular haircut, and another veranda called the “Sinners Gallery” (in Spanish) where the general plotted and gossiped. Folklore was thrown in too, about the kapre in the mango tree that warned Aguinaldo when danger was nearby. Linda made the general more than a maligned name in our textbook history; he became human. When she was in grade school, she asked her lolo about his participation in Andres Bonifacio’s death, his evasive reply: “pagtanda mo hija, maintindihan mo ang mga pangyayari noon.”

Apolinario Mabini has two national shrines: in his birthplace in Barrio Talaga, Tanauan, Batangas, and the house where he passed away, formerly near Nagtahan Bridge, now in the Polytechnic University of the Philippines Mabini campus. The Nagtahan Shrine was run by Apolinario Mabini III, a descendant of Mabini’s brother, affectionately called “Ka Pule.” I remember looking over Mabini’s wheelchair, his eyeglasses, and tattered old books, some bearing Mabini’s signature or notes. Mabini read Spanish and English; one of the books in his library was by Arthur Conan Doyle but not from the Sherlock Holmes series. Ka Pule asked a pointed question that has resonated with me both as a historian and a collector. Why, he asked ruefully, are Jose Rizal’s things valued more than the mementoes of other heroes? “Why do Rizal relics sell way more than Mabini’s?” “Bakit pag gamit ni Rizal mahal,” Ka Pule said with a shrug, “‘pag gamit ni Mabini mura?” Sad to say, in an important lot of papers I was consulted on some years back, Rizal’s letters were valued in seven figures while all of Mabini’s remained unsold, even if they were valued at a fraction of Rizal’s. Andres Bonifacio’s papers draw as much attention as Rizal’s because these are scarce, but why did the handwritten memoirs of his widow Gregoria de Jesus remain unsold at auction?

Of the two competing auction houses in Manila today, Leon Gallery leads in the sale of historical material: books, manuscripts, maps, ephemera. Historians will not find these in archives, libraries, or museums, but if they take the trouble to visit during presale viewing hours as I do, they can take advantage of the short window when the items pass from one private collection only to disappear into another private collection

People have been asking my opinion on a pair of epaulets or shoulder insignia said to belong to the ill-fated Gen. Antonio Luna. They are embroidered on red silk with silver thread by artisans who craft vestments for religious images. It is not well-known that the insignia of officer’s uniforms during the Philippine-American War was designed by Juan Luna. Based on his designs, Antonio Luna’s epaulets or “galones” in Spanish correspond to a two-star “Teniente General.” Higher than one-star “General de Brigada” or “General de Division,” lower than the three-star “Capitan General” reserved for Emilio Aguinaldo.

I was naturally skeptical. Were these epaulets of another general? If they are Antonio Luna’s, these carry the drama of his bloody death. I saw what was said to be Antonio Luna’s bloodied uniform before it burned in an art gallery fire in the 1980s. In retrospect, I should have examined the blue rayadillo uniform more thoroughly and counted the bullet and knife holes. I was a college student then, not today’s historian obsessed with detail. That uniform did not have epaulets. The trail of ownership or provenance is an undated, signed, and typewritten certification from Florentina Arellano Vda. de Nable who was on the staff of La Independencia, whose editor in chief was Antonio Luna.

Florentina recalls that on June 5, 1899, Antonio Luna received a telegram from Aguinaldo inviting him to Cabanatuan for a meeting. Before leaving Dagupan, Antonio Luna requested a “merienda china” and his friend Mariano Arellano had one prepared. Antonio Luna hardly ate, saying, “I don’t know what’s happening to me, I’m sad and a bitter premonition dominates me.” His aide-de-camp Paco Roman felt the same. “I’m not sick,” Paco said, “but feel terribly afflicted. My heart beats rapidly. I feel something grave will happen to me.” On his way to the carriage, Antonio remarked, “I forgot my epaulets in the sala, on top of the piano. Take care of them in case I return (por si acaso vuelvo).”

Florentina recalls all these details in retrospect, including the unlucky number of guests at the table that day—13. Come to think of it, these are just old objects, until they connect to history or a historical person. Those are the stories of history.
Comments are welcome at ambeth.ocampo@inquirer.net

articles.title: The kids are not alright—but our targets say otherwise
articles.summary: A government target is not just a number. It tells us what problems the government recognizes, what success means, and what it is prepared to fund. That is why some targets in the proposed 2027…

blocks.text: A government target is not just a number. It tells us what problems the government recognizes, what success means, and what it is prepared to fund. That is why some targets in the proposed 2027 National Expenditure Program (NEP) deserve scrutiny. Unless properly aligned, they risk letting agencies claim success on paper even as the condition of Filipino children worsens.

Nutrition: Hitting the target, missing the child. The 2025 Department of Science and Technology-Food and Nutrition Research Institute (DOST-FNRI) survey found 25.3 percent of children under 5 are stunted, up from 23.6 percent in 2023—the first national increase in over a decade. The Philippine Development Plan (PDP) retained targets to cut stunting to 20.8 percent in 2026, 19.4 percent in 2027, and 17.9 percent by 2028, while the National Education and Workforce Development Plan targets below 10 percent by 2035.

This is ambitious but not unprecedented: Indonesia cut stunting from 37.2 percent (2013) to 19.8 percent (2024); Bangladesh from 42 percent (2013) to 24 percent (2025); Vietnam from 29.3 percent (2010) to 19.6 percent (2019). Yet these national outcomes no longer appear among the National Nutrition Council’s (NNC) agency indicators. Stunting and wasting were direct indicators in 2022-2023 General Appropriations Act; by 2024 they were marked “not applicable,” and by 2025 replaced by indicators on local government units’ (LGU) scores, message recall, policies, and stakeholders assisted.

These may reflect real agency activity, but they may also obscure the key question that matters: are fewer children becoming stunted? While national stunting rose to 25.3 percent, NNC reported 96.16 percent of evaluated (LGU) meeting the minimum “Seal of Quality Nutrition” score, against a target of only 20 percent. This presents a conflicting picture: of an agency seemingly overachieving their original target, while in reality, stunting is worsening.

As Senators Bam Aquino and Alan Peter Cayetano also discussed on the floor last week, the datasets also conflict sharply: NNC’s 2025 Operation Timbang Plus reports stunting at about 5 percent, versus FNRI’s 25.3 percent. Both systems have value, but a fivefold gap cannot go unexplained—government must clarify who was counted, who was missed, and which figure actually governs planning and accountability.

ECCD Council: Counting the program, not the children. In 2025, the Early Childhood Care and Development (ECCD) Council reported an 81-percent accomplishment against an 85-percent enrollment target. But that meant computing participation for only 32,241 out of a 40,000 target—strikingly, under 1 percent of the roughly 4.5 million Filipino children aged 3 to 4. To illustrate, 40,000 is about the size of an urbanized city’s population for ages 3-4, but not the millions the ECCD system is meant to serve nationwide. Their denominator has also shifted repeatedly, from 4,500 in 2022 to 50,300 in 2026, possibly reflecting target populations rather than national participation targets.

Today, participation in ECCD is only 34 percent, while Republic Act No. 12199 mandates universal early childhood access for all children under 5. Laudably, the council’s proposed 2027 indicators finally adopt national participation targets—40 percent for ages 3 to under 5, 2 percent for under 3—although still falling short of the PDP’s 50-percent target for 2027.

Keeping our targets honest. Both cases point to a larger problem: performance indicators can reward agencies for counting what’s convenient rather than for changing the conditions they exist to address. As a result, budgets may also risk funding the size of programs instead of the true scale of the problem.

These indicators made it into the proposed 2027 budget, raising an unavoidable question: who vets the targets under the NEP to ensure that they are not disconnected from national outcomes, and are consistent with the PDP? To what extent do the targets relate to the budgets proposed?

Target-setting is shared work—agencies bring sector expertise, Department of Budget and Management (DBM) ties targets to appropriations and performance, Department of Economy, Planning, and Development (DepDev) safeguards alignment with national priorities—but shared responsibility must not mean diluted accountability. DBM and DepDev should challenge targets that are too narrow, disconnected from national plans, or incapable of showing whether conditions are actually improving.

As Congress deliberates, agencies must show how meeting their targets represents genuine national progress, not just administrative compliance. Accountability begins with the basics: the right target, an honest baseline, and a clear accounting of the resources required to deliver it. They should publish bases for denominators, reconcile conflicting datasets, and demonstrate how requested funds will move real outcomes.
Changing an indicator does not change the child. When agencies, national plans, and local governments define success differently, accountability is diluted, even as everyone appears compliant.
The kids are not alright. Our targets must be honest enough to say so.
Dr. Karol Mark Yee is the executive director of the Second Congressional Commission on Education.

articles.title: COA’s anticorruption mandate
articles.summary: The testimony of auditors of the Commission on Audit (COA) in the ongoing impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte showed the significant role the COA plays in safeguarding the people’s…

blocks.text: The testimony of auditors of the Commission on Audit (COA) in the ongoing impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte showed the significant role the COA plays in safeguarding the people’s money.
The auditors disclosed the various schemes the Vice President used to account for her use (or misuse) of millions of pesos in confidential funds that were given to her office.
They were able to successfully parry the attempts of the defense lawyer and some senator-judges to minimize the significance of their audit findings. Indeed, they were not auditors for nothing.
Sadly, the COA’s investigation of those transactions was limited to reviewing the acknowledged receipts and other documents submitted to supposedly liquidate the disbursed funds.

Unlike the Bureau of Internal Revenue, the country’s primary revenue collection agency, the COA does not have the personnel and facilities that can cross-check and verify the veracity of the documents submitted by the government offices it audits.

Note that the COA and Office of the Ombudsman (OMB) are constitutional offices that have been specifically mandated to watch over government offices to make sure they efficiently perform their duties and responsibilities, including the proper use of public funds.
To the credit of the OMB, it has, since the appointment of Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla, been making a good account of itself in its anticorruption activities.

With regard to the COA, in a recent budget hearing at the House of Representatives, COA assistant commissioner Lorna Cabochan expressed concern about her office’s capability to perform its mandate due to shortage of field auditors.

She said the COA needs 384 more auditors, plus additional funds for, among others, its Information Systems Strategic Plan, the construction or modernization of some of its buildings and the purchase of three motor vehicles.

(Incidentally, on top of budgetary constraints, the recruitment of additional auditors could be challenging considering that many Filipino accountants prefer to handle online accounting and auditing work assignments from companies based abroad that give higher pay, plus the ability to work from home.)

As things stand at present, the Department of Budget and Management (DBM) does not seem inclined to grant the COA’s requests, not even to fund the purchase of a car for the COA’s office in the Negros Island Region. (What a bummer!)
The DBM’s lukewarm, if not dismissive, response to the COA’s “wish list,” couldn’t have come at the worst of times. Talk of bad timing.

Note that in the past months, the flood control projects scandal has been in the public eye and the floods that recently hit Metro Manila, Bulacan, and Pampanga, among others, showed the reality of the adverse effects of the scam perpetrated by some members of Congress in cooperation with their private contractors’ cohorts.

At the height of the typhoon, social media was replete with posts asking why, in spite of the billions in pesos allocated and spent for flood control projects, floods of unprecedented proportions had not been prevented, if not minimized to manageable levels.
Take a look at Bulacan.

The COA earlier reported that last year, only two auditors were assigned to the Department of Public Works and Highways’ engineering office in Bulacan, which has become the template for flood control corruption.
Aside from Bulacan, there are other areas in the country that are believed to have been inflicted with the same damage by their congressional representatives.

In a manner of speaking, the surface has barely been scratched to unravel the flood control projects that some members of Congress have used as a mechanism to line their pockets with the people’s money.
They await the audit findings needed to support the filing of complaints for misappropriation of public funds or, worse, the nonbailable crime of plunder.

Unless the COA’s corps of field auditors is beefed up immediately, the thorough audit investigation of those areas may have to be indefinitely deferred or done in spurts, giving the people behind the scandal time to falsify documents or make them disappear to avoid getting caught.
Digging through tons of paperwork to see if the proper procedures have been complied with in the disposition of the people’s money is like looking for a needle in a haystack.

And once an apparent violation is found and the government official concerned is made to explain, the auditor would have to practically do a reprise of what he or she had done earlier and more if the government official concerned happens to be politically influential.
It’s a task that requires a lot of patience, dedication, and expertise. And the COA auditors have shown they are up to it.
If the government wants COA to accomplish its constitutional mandate, it should give it the appropriate staff and instruments for that purpose.
raul.palabrica@inquirer.net

articles.title: Nothing is impossible if we unite for our country
articles.summary: What can we learn from the current world situation for the Philippines? We can learn about survival from countries like Iran and Cuba. While it’s always militarily advantageous and provides a…

blocks.text: What can we learn from the current world situation for the Philippines?

We can learn about survival from countries like Iran and Cuba. While it’s always militarily advantageous and provides a political safety net to be a nuclear power like Russia, China, or North Korea, it also requires the will to suffer. But if that will is there, then miracles are possible, like David versus Goliath. Iran is a case in point, increasingly dictating peace negotiations with the “superpower” United States.

It’s not just cynics who are now saying that Iran has essentially won the war against the US and emerged stronger than before. Looking at its current position, one can certainly agree. US President Donald Trump must put the unpopular and expensive war behind him before the US midterms, otherwise he will become the proverbial “lame duck” for his last two years in office.

But someone who has nothing to lose can become very dangerous. Even the Cubans, in their tragic, externally imposed situation, have proven through cunning and practical resistance that they can survive not only for the last few months but for almost 70 years now.

What did all this mean for the Philippines? What can we learn from it? First, nothing is impossible. A people with a high capacity for suffering can work miracles. However, there is a caveat: if corruption and clans gain the upper hand over patriotism and brotherhood, then fairy tales come to an end.
At the moment, this “unity” reminds me more of the deeply divided US, split into two hostile camps. But we shouldn’t be concerned with the US; the Philippines should be our only love.

Like many other commentators, I also doubt that the US is still a reliable partner today. Just ask the European Nato members or countries in the Middle East. But sometimes history repeats itself. Tiny Vietnam also triumphed over the US. The US had to flee the country in 1975, much like in Afghanistan in 2021. Small, seemingly weak countries can therefore achieve a great deal if they unite in their resistance, rise above themselves, and reinvent themselves.

Can the Philippines do that? Looking ahead to the 2028 elections, I unfortunately fear the opposite. Albert Einstein once answered the question about the meaning of life with practical philosophy: “A person’s worth is shown by what they give, not by what they can take.”

The revolutionary Che Guevara expressed it this way: “Always be capable of feeling deep within yourself every injustice against everyone, anywhere in the world; then act in fraternal solidarity.” The best thing to do is start with ourselves, right now.
Jürgen Schöfer, Ph.D.,
Biopreparat.Schoefer@gmail.com

articles.title: Edmonton woman convicted in fatal dog attack that killed 11-year-old sentenced to house arrest
articles.summary: An Edmonton woman who owned two large Cane Corso dogs that killed an 11-year-old boy in 2024 has been sentenced. Crystal Jean MacDonald, 46, was found guilty of criminal negligence causing death in…

image.caption: Kache Grist is shown in this handout photo provided by his mother Kendrah Wong. (The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Edmonton

An Edmonton woman who owned two large Cane Corso dogs that killed an 11-year-old boy in 2024 has been sentenced. Crystal Jean MacDonald, 46, was found guilty of criminal negligence causing death in May following a judge-alone trial at the Edmonton Court of King’s Bench.
Kache Grist was attacked by dogs at a south Edmonton home in 2024
An Edmonton woman who owned two large Cane Corso dogs that killed an 11-year-old boy in 2024 will serve a conditional house arrest sentence of two years less a day, a judge decided Thursday.

Crystal Jean MacDonald, 46, was found guilty of criminal negligence causing death in May following a judge-alone trial at the Edmonton Court of King’s Bench. Kache Grist was killed on April 1, 2024 after MacDonald's two dogs attacked him.
Justice Eric Macklin sentenced MacDonald on Thursday. Her conditions include a lifetime ban on owning, supervising, or controlling dogs. She can apply for a leave on this condition in 10 years.
She is also subject to complete 200 hours of community service.

Macklin listed aggravating factors that include MacDonald not properly training her dogs, the previous attacks on humans and the death of two pets, the age and vulnerability of Kache, and the manner of death being “horrific.” But Macklin noted she had showed concern for Kache, there was no intent on her behalf and she had demonstrated “great remorse.”
MacDonald will serve her sentence in Penticton, B.C.
Crown prosecutors sought a five-year incarceration sentence, while defence sought a conditional sentence for two years less a day.

During sentencing Wednesday, court heard an emotional victim impact statement delivered virtually from Kache’s father, Wesley Grist, who described his son as the most important person in his life and part of his identity.
“The grief is constant,” he read to the courtroom adding that he believes that situation was a tragic circumstance.
He told the court that he never wanted revenge for his son's death and MacDonald will be carrying the weight of his death.
“At no point was my testimony given with anger,” he said. “I never wanted harm to come to her [MacDonald], I know she loved Kache.
“Nothing about this feels like a victory to me.”
MacDonald was also given the opportunity to address the court. Through tears she explained the guilt, grief, and shame she feels.
“I love Kache deeply,” she said. “I think about him every single day.”
“I don’t know how to explain what it feels like to be standing here because of the death of a child that I love,” she said.
Kache’s mother, Kendrah Wong was present in the courtroom Wednesday. Wong submitted a victim impact statement but requested for it to be read privately.
Trial testimonies

MacDonald owned two Cane Corso dogs, Khaos and Khairo, which have since been euthanized. Court heard Khaos weighed about 56 kilograms (124 pounds) and Khairo weighed more than 49 kilograms (109 pounds) at the time of the attack.
During the trial, court heard Kache Grist was visiting his father, Wesley Grist, in Edmonton from Osoyoos, B.C., for spring break and staying at MacDonald’s south Edmonton home.
Wesley testified that on April 1, 2024, his son briefly left the home to buy snacks at a nearby Circle K.
MacDonald was not home at the time.
Grist said he was working in the garage while the dogs remained inside. Kache returned from the convenience store and went inside to play video games.
Grist testified that MacDonald had previously warned him to keep Kache away from the dogs and not to leave him alone with them.
An autopsy found Kache died from a dog-bite injury to the neck. The autopsy also documented injuries to his upper back, shoulders and arms.
During the trial, court heard about previous attacks involving the dogs, including an attack on MacDonald herself, an acquaintance and a former tenant. The dogs had also fatally attacked two pets.

MacDonald testified that she knew the dogs had shown aggressive behaviour before Kache’s death, but believed she had taken steps to manage them, including kennelling them and seeking professional training.
She maintained that some of the previous attacks could have been prevented if people had followed the rules she had established for the dogs.

When Macklin delivered his decision in May, he found the most significant cause of Kache’s death was the failure of MacDonald to take the reasonable steps to ensure that he was not harmed by the two untrained and unpredictable dogs.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Jesmeen Gill is a reporter for CBC News in Edmonton. She is a recent graduate from Carleton University’s journalism program in Ottawa and has previously interned at The Canadian Press. You can reach her at jesmeen.gill@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Australia news live: Pauline Hanson to make cost of living ‘worse’, new union boss warns; Labor scraps course citing ‘integrity’
articles.summary:
The new ACTU secretary, Melissa Donnelly, says One Nation ‘says one thing and does another’

  • Get our breaking news…

blocks.text: Key events

items: 2m agoWorkers should have a say in when and how AI is used, ACTU secretary says
23m agoWelcome

blocks.caption: Josh Taylor

blocks.text: Josh Taylor
Asked if she saw her role as one of countering One Nation on the cost of living, Donnelly said Pauline Hanson’s party “says one thing and does another”.

double quotation markThe reality is that Pauline Hanson’s track record is voting against penalty rates, voting against rights for casual and gig workers. She’s opposed the minimum wage. She’s most recently suggested it should be easier to sack workers. Our job, as the union movement, is to make sure our members and workers understand that is what she stands for. And if you’re worried about cost of living, Pauline Hanson is going to make it worse.
Workers should have a say in when and how AI is used, ACTU secretary says
The new secretary of the Australian Council of Trade Unions, Melissa Donnelly, has said cost of living issues and the rollout of AI in workplaces are two major focuses of her new role.
Donnelly told ABC’s 7.30 program workers “absolutely deserve” a say on AI in their workplaces, but it would not amount to a veto.
She said unions will test the existing laws demanding workers are consulted over significant impacts of new technology before suggesting the laws need to be strengthened for AI.
double quotation markThere are a whole range of workplace issues, and workers’ rights issues, that arise with the advent of AI.
The stronger guardrails Donnelly said, would include the capacity of workers to have a say on “when it’s used and how it’s used”.

double quotation markThere’s a broader conversation that we should be having as a nation about what AI means and how we regulate it. It’s not a tropical cyclone bearing down on the coast. It is technology. We’ve seen governments step in on issues like social media and set some guardrails. We have all sorts of commentators from Bill Gates to others saying that we’ve got to have some rules around how this works, we’ve got to have protections, because we need to protect workers into there future. We need to make sure there are meaningful and quality jobs going forward.

blocks.caption: Krishani Dhanji

blocks.text: Krishani Dhanji
Labor says it will shut down a management course amid fears it is being “misused by shonks” and providing a back door into Australia.

As the government faces increased pressure to curb overseas migration, Labor says the graduate diploma of management (learning) which is registered at 452 institutions showed students either were enrolled but weren’t even starting the course, weren’t completing the course or were transferring out of it.
It’s the first time the government will use powers to shut down courses due to concerns over their integrity – though students currently completing the course will be able to finish it.
The assistant minister in charge, Julian Hill, pinned the blame on the Coalition:

double quotation markThe Coalition left behind a shocking mess in 2022, with unsustainably high growth in student numbers in the least reputable parts of the sector, and our high-quality student visa being degraded into a low-rent illegal work visa and misused by shonks. Australia continues to welcome genuine international students seeking a premium education and must maintain a ruthless focus on quality, integrity and a great student experience.
Welcome
Good morning and welcome to our live news blog. I’m Martin Farrer with the top overnight stories and then it will be Nick Visser with the main action.

The new secretary of the Australian Council of Trade Unions, Melissa Donnelly, has said cost of living issues and the rollout of AI in workplaces are two major focuses of her new role. More coming up.

articles.title: Alex Eala rolls past Oleksandra Oliynykova into US Open third round
articles.summary: LIVE: Alex Eala vs Oleksandra Oliynykova – US Open 2026 second round MANILA, Philippines–Alex Eala marched on to the third round of the US Open 2026 after turning back Oleksandra Oliynykova of…

blocks.text: Philippines’ Alexandra Eala celebrates defeating Ukraine’s Oleksandra Oliynykova during their women’s singles second-round tennis match on day five of the US Open tennis tournament at the USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center in New York on September 3, 2026. (Photo by TIMOTHY A. CLARY / AFP)
LIVE: Alex Eala vs Oleksandra Oliynykova – US Open 2026 second round
MANILA, Philippines–Alex Eala marched on to the third round of the US Open 2026 after turning back Oleksandra Oliynykova of Ukraine, 6-1, 6-4 on Friday at Louis Armstrong Stadium in New York.
Eala built on her blazing start to withstand Oliynykova’s comeback in the second set and surpass her breakthrough second-round finish at Flushing Meadows last year.
“I think my patience and the consistency of my focus–I think that was the key to winning the match today,” Eala said in the on-court interview.
She faces Iva Jovic, who ousted Francesca Jones, 6-4, 6-4, in their own second-round match, in the Round of 32.
Eala, the world No. 18 and 17th seed, won the first eight points to race to a 2-0 lead before building a 4-0 advantage and wrapping up the set, 6-1, in just 23 minutes.

blocks.caption: Alexandra Eala, of the Philippines, reacts during the second round of the U.S. Open tennis championships against Oleksandra Oliynykova, of Ukraine, Thursday, Sept. 3, 2026, in New York

blocks.text: Alexandra Eala, of the Philippines, reacts during the second round of the U.S. Open tennis championships against Oleksandra Oliynykova, of Ukraine, Thursday, Sept. 3, 2026, in New York. (AP Photo/Seth Wenig)
But the world No. 46 Oliynykova, who beat Eala last May on clay at the Strasbourg Open, came out with a steadier service game in the second set and took an early 2-1 lead.
Eala responded with a love hold and the first break of the second set to regain the advantage at 3-2 before Oliynykova broke back to tie it.
A break and a love service game pushed Eala closer to victory at 5-3. Oliynykova won a game to stay in contention, but the Eala served out the match to the delight of the Filipino fans.

“I think everybody represents something in their own way. I’m Filipino and I proudly represent that and a lot of the crowd here today is Filipino and I’m sure they share in that sentiment,” Eala said.
It was Eala’s second straight match at the second-largest stadium at the USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center, following her opening-round win over Mary Stoiana, also in straight sets.
Eala continues her impressive showing in the same city where she won her first Grand Slam title as a junior.
